Political disputes must not affect Indus treaty: experts. • Participants urge Pakistan to continue adhering to accord • Munir Akram calls for active diplomacy, continued use of agreement mechanisms • Rizwan Saeed says treaty faces a ‘crisis of intent’ • Sherry says India can’t unilaterally suspend or reinterpret treaty WASHINGTON: Pakistan should not allow political and security disputes to become a justification for departing from the Indus Waters Treaty, participants at a policy dialogue in Washington said, stressing that such issues should be dealt with separately. The speakers rejected India’s position that the treaty would remain in abeyance until violence in the region ceased, arguing that water-sharing arrangements should remain separate from political and security disputes and that the treaty’s provisions should continue to govern management of the Indus river system. The observation came during a discussion on the future of the treaty hosted by the Pakistan Embassy, with participants warning against allowing political tensions to undermine an agreement that has survived wars and repeated crises between Pakistan and India. The dialogue, titled “The Indus Waters Treaty: South Asian Security at Crossroads”, brought together US policy experts, academics, legal and water specialists, representatives of international organisations and diplomats to examine the treaty’s future and growing challenges to regional water security. Former Pakistan ambassador to the United Nations Munir Akram said Pakistan should continue to abide by the treaty despite current tensions, arguing that India’s decision to place it in abeyance did not alter its legal status. “Pakistan shouldn’t depart from the letter and spirit of the treaty,” he said. Mr Akram also argued that Pakistan needed an active diplomatic strategy in response to India’s position and should continue participating in treaty mechanisms even if New Delhi refused to do so. He suggested exploring the creation of an impartial international mechanism, including a possible role for the United Nations, and said Pakistan should also consult China, which he viewed as being in a position to influence the outcome. The discussion repeatedly returned to the need to preserve the treaty’s legal and institutional framework. Participants noted that the Indus Waters Treaty had survived wars, crises and prolonged political tensions and had helped keep water cooperation insulated from disputes. Pakistan’s ambassador to the United States Rizwan Saeed Sheikh said Islamabad had consistently favoured dialogue, diplomacy and peaceful coexistence, pointing to its efforts to facilitate dialogue over other regional disputes. “If we can do it for others, we will do it for ourselves,” he said, referring to Pakistan’s efforts to help resolve the Iran-US dispute. He also urged India to remain engaged with Pakistan, saying: “You cannot change neighbours, so we want to engage in constructive dialogue.” In his concluding remarks, Mr Sheikh said the problem with the Indus Waters Treaty was not its substance but the manner in which it was being implemented. “There is no crisis of content in the Indus Waters Treaty … there is a crisis of intent in implementation,” he said. Adil Najam, professor of international relations and dean emeritus at Boston University, said the treaty defined the future of water cooperation in South Asia and stressed the importance of cooperation in managing shared resources. He said climate change and increasing water stress should encourage, rather than undermine, cooperation between countries sharing water resources. Participants also cautioned against dehumanising the other side, with one speaker noting that there were “many sensible people in India” and arguing that the two countries needed to look for practical solutions despite their political differences. The discussion examined whether the current dispute was primarily political or legal, with legal experts stressing the importance of international law and established dispute-resolution mechanisms. Speakers also warned about the consequences of treating water as an instrument of political or military pressure. A large share of Pakistan’s population and economy depend on the Indus river system, participants noted, raising concerns about the regional consequences if water were weaponised. The nuclear dimension of the dispute was also discussed, with participants cautioning against assumptions that nuclear deterrence alone would prevent escalation. Mr Najam noted that despite the lack of trust between India and Pakistan, the treaty had worked for decades and argued that the priority should be to prevent the existing framework from falling apart. Participants also stressed the importance of restoring technical engagement, transparency and data-sharing between Pakistan and India under the treaty’s provisions, particularly as climate change and growing water stress place additional pressure on the region’s shared resources. Sherry calls for full compliance Separately, PPP Vice President and parliamentary leader in the Senate Sherry Rehman urged India to ensure full compliance with the Indus Waters Treaty, warning that the politicisation of water and its use as a tool of diplomatic pressure threatened regional stability and undermined decades of bilateral water cooperation. Senator Rehman said India could not unilaterally suspend, disregard or reinterpret a decades-old bilateral water management framework at will. She said any decision to withdraw from or suspend an international agreement could not be made through a unilateral declaration, but had to be undertaken in accordance with established procedures of international law. “The Indian government’s recent actions cannot, in any manner, undermine Pakistan’s legitimate rights and interests concerning its water resources,” she said. Senator Rehman stressed that taking the legal dispute to international forums was not a compulsion for Pakistan but a lawful right available to it under the established international framework. She said India could not use its water and hydropower projects as a pretext to disregard internationally agreed principles and limitations governing the shared river system. Iftikhar A. Khan in Islamabad also contributed to this report Published in Dawn, August 30th, 2026

AJK PM vows to restore internet, road links in days. MUZAFFARABAD: Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) Prime Minister Barrister Iftikhar Gillani has assured the business community and students that his government would restore internet services at educational institutions and remove restrictions on road links with Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa within the next few days. Speaking during his visit to the Central Press Club on Saturday, Mr Gillani said the government was also working on a policy to address the losses suffered by the business community, particularly in Mirpur, due to the internet shutdown and recent protests. “We will try to restore business activity and help recover the losses,” he said. PM Gillani, who was accompanied by fellow legislators Chaudhry Abdul Rehman Arain and Dr Mustafa Bashir Abbasi, expressed concern over the situation in Rawalakot , saying his government would make every effort to bring it under control. He said the educational loss being suffered by children was the government’s foremost concern, as teaching activities had been disrupted in educational institutions. “I will make every effort to have internet services restored in educational institutions within the next few days,” he said. He also assured the public that restrictions on routes connecting AJK with Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa would be removed within a day or two. “I assure you that these closures will no longer be visible anywhere in the next one or two days. There will be no restrictions or hindrances of any kind on movement,” he declared. The prime minister said his government wanted to bring political forces and the people of the state together to move AJK forward. “If the government is genuinely interested in resolving the problems of the people, there should be nothing that creates discord within the state or sends a message of division to the outside world,” he said. Gillani leaves for Lahore to meet Nawaz, Maryam Mr Gillani said the election of a number of young PML-N legislators had brought a “clear change” to the political landscape and expressed confidence in his team’s ability to deliver. “Our entire team has the ability to deliver. It has delivered in the past and will deliver again, and you will all see that delivery,” he said. Referring to development in AJK, the prime minister credited former prime minister Nawaz Sharif with doubling the region’s development budget, saying the increase had enabled people to see tangible development. He said the building of the Central Press Club was also made possible by the resources provided by the PML-N federal government. Mr Gillani thanked Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif for establishing Danish schools in four AJK districts. He described the initiative as a manifestation of the PML-N leadership’s “affection” for the people of AJK. He also appealed to the media to help create a positive environment and play its role in countering what he described as negative effects. “This is also the purpose of my visit to the Press Club today,” he said, adding that society needed to move beyond the pursuit of “fame and views” and join hands to build a strong, educated and developed AJK. Earlier, Mr Gillani visited the terminal of the green electric buses provided to AJK by Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz. Senior Member Board of Revenue Sardar Mohammad Zafar and other officials briefed him on the proposed launch of the bus service, its routes and other arrangements. The prime minister inspected the e-buses and reviewed facilities at the terminal, issuing directions to the officials concerned. Speaking on the occasion, Mr Gillani thanked PML-N President Nawaz Sharif and CM Maryam for fulfilling their commitment to provide green buses to AJK before the elections. He said the PML-N government’s objective was to promote development, ensure public welfare and reduce people’s hardships. “I assure the people of Azad Kashmir that the PML-N government will work to reduce their problems and address their sense of deprivation. We will make every effort to improve their lives and ensure that the people feel the difference of having a PML-N government in place,” he said. Later, Mr Gillani left for Lahore on Saturday, where his key engagement would be a courtesy call on party supremo Nawaz Sharif and CM Maryam on Sunday. Published in Dawn, August 30th, 2026

Putin, Xi, Pezeshkian to attend Kyrgyzstan summit. BISHKEK: Russia’s Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping are expected in Central Asia’s Kyrgyzstan on Monday for a two-day summit, also attended by Pakistan, Iran and India’s leaders, of a regional bloc seeking to be a counter-influence to the West. Around a dozen heads of states will head to the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek to mark 25 years of the Shanghai Cooperation Group (SCO). The group brings together Russia, China, India, Pakistan, Iran, four Central Asian countries and Moscow-allied Belarus. It takes place four-and-a-half years into Moscow’s Ukraine invasion and six months into the war between Washington and Tehran . Iran will be represented by its president, Masoud Pezeshkian. PM Shehbaz and Modi to join them at SCO event Putin, Xi, Pezeshkian as well as India’s Narendra Modi and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif are due to take part in a plenary session chaired by Kyrgyz leader Sadyr Japarov. Putin is also expected to hold separate bilateral talks with Pezeshkian and Xi, among other leaders, Kremlin spokesman Yuri Ushakov said. Russia and Iran, among the most sanctioned states in the world, have massively deepened their military and economic ties during the Ukraine war. US President Donald Trump has warned Moscow and Beijing against arming Iran. Putin’s meeting with Pezeshkian comes days after the CIA’s director John Ratcliffe made a rare trip to Moscow, with US media speculating he could have discussed Ukraine and Iran with his Russian counterparts. The SCO has historically focused on economic issues. It gained momentum in recent years under Moscow’s and Beijing’s leadership. The SCO’s founding declaration says the group is “not an alliance directed against other states”. Real and trade wars The Bishkek summit takes place as some SCO members are in the midst of real wars — the Ukraine and Iran conflicts — or trade wars, with the imposition of US tariffs on Chinese and Indian goods. Mohammad Hassan Najmi, an international relations expert, told AFP that Tehran “believes its membership and active participation in these alliances can enable it to circumvent US and European sanctions”. But concrete benefits of the group are uncertain, he said, as “in times of crisis, these alliances have rarely allowed Iran to resolve its difficulties”. While the bloc claims to represent some 40 per cent of the world’s population and 25pc of global GDP, it remains diverse, with some disagreements among members. Published in Dawn, August 30th, 2026

GB sees rise in foreign climbers, trekkers despite Mideast tensions. • Over 2,200 adventurers visited region from April to August • Official says climbing season has closed, but trekking will continue until October GILGIT: More than 2,200 foreign climbers and trekkers visited Gilgit-Baltistan during the summer season from April to August this year, a senior official of the GB Tourism Department said. Sajid Hussain, deputy director of the GB Tourism Department, told Dawn that foreign adventurers visited the region to scale some of the world’s highest peaks and trek in restricted areas, including K2 (8,611 metres), Nanga Parbat (8,126m), Broad Peak (8,047m), Gasherbrum-I (8,080m) and Gasherbrum-II (8,035m). The official added that a large number of foreign and domestic tourists were currently visiting popular destinations across Gilgit-Baltistan. Foreign tourists visiting open-zone areas do not require permits. Officials said foreign tourists visiting GB’s tourist destinations and open-zone areas from multiple countries during the spring, summer and autumn seasons were expected to surpass 10,000 this year. Mr Hussain said the number of foreign adventurers visiting GB this summer was higher than last year. The official said tensions following the US-Israel war on Iran, as well as a fuel price hike, had affected the influx of foreign and domestic tourists to GB last year. Mr Hussain said the climbing season had now closed, although trekkers continued to visit restricted areas, including the K2 Base Camp trekking route. “The arrival of trekkers will continue until October,” he said. The Gilgit-Baltistan government earned Rs350 million from expedition and trekking pe­­rmits during the summer season up to June 30. President of the Alpine Club of Pakistan, retired Major General Irfan Arshad Khan, told Dawn that the surge in international tourists this year, despite uncertainty in the Middle East , fluctuations in fuel prices and other factors, was encouraging. “Tourism is a source of employment for the people of GB. Besides the revenue collected through trekking and mountaineering fees, local people, including porters, hotel owners, transporters and shopkeepers, benefit by millions of dollars directly from tourists,” he said. “Following the war in the Middle East and the law-and-order situation in Pakistan after the assassination of Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei during US and Israeli attacks on Iran, many countries issued advisories to their citizens against travelling to Pakistan. There were also delays in the issuance of permits for foreign climbers and trekkers. Otherwise, the number of foreign adventurers visiting GB would have been higher than 2,200,” Major General Irfan Arshad Khan said. He said more than 4,000 foreign climbers and trekkers were expected to visit the region next year. He said the flaws causing delays in the issuance of permits to foreigners and other related issues would be resolved. However, the summit success rate on major peaks in GB, including K2, Broad Peak, Gasherbrum-I, Gasherbrum-II and Nanga Parbat, remained low because of snow avalanches, rockfalls, high winds and unpredictable weather conditions at high altitudes. Published in Dawn, August 30th, 2026

Steep challenge. AN abundance of good fortune has landed a 46-year-old barrister, Syed Iftikhar Ali Gillani, in the hot seat. He will serve as the 17th prime minister of Azad Jammu and Kashmir, having been elected to the post on Friday with 30 votes from his party, the PML-N. For now, Mr Gillani heads an incomplete legislative assembly, with seven seats representing the Poonch and Sudhnoti districts yet to be filled due to the law-and-order situation in those areas. He made note of that fact in his inaugural speech, hoping that the remainder of the electoral process will be completed soon. He also promised employment, especially for the youth, recruitment on merit, transparency and anti-corruption measures, improvement in education and healthcare, digitising the economy, and launching a portal to address citizens’ grievances. That makes for a bold, positive start to what is bound to be a challenging assignment. Mr Gillani will remain under constant scrutiny, including from his own party. The recent general election in AJK has remained marred by controversy. There were frequent and vociferous accusations of impropriety and alleged rigging , including from one of the PML-N’s most important allies at the centre. The AJK Election Commission, too, controversially decided it would declare voting results after each phase of the election, raising serious questions regarding electoral propriety. And then there were the large-scale and often violent protests that disrupted the process, which have yet to be conclusively addressed. To top it off, Mr Gillani’s candidature for the premiership also drew strong resistance from within his own party. Senior PML-N figures, including the AJK chapter president Shah Ghulam Qadir and former AJK prime minister Raja Farooq Haider, openly and strongly opposed his nomination. Mr Qadir had been considered the leading contender before Mr Gillani’s entry, but the party seems to have had other plans. Critics also pointed to the fact that Mr Gillani lost the Muzaffarabad-III constituency he had contested in the general election and was only returned to the AJK Legislative Assembly on a reserved technocrat seat. This clashed with the PML-N’s own position on ‘respecting the vote’, as the critics pointed out. Still, it appears that the party’s central leadership insisted on a younger face over the old guard in AJK. Whether that bet pays off remains to be seen. Mr Gillani will need to prove his doubters wrong while placating those elements in AJK that resisted or boycotted the electoral process. The latter may be the most sensitive aspect of his job, given the criticality of restoring stability in the region. He has been involved in AJK politics at least since 2010, and has previously served in the AJK cabinet. Whether or not those experiences have prepared him adequately for the premiership will soon become evident. Published in Dawn, August 30th, 2026

Durbar legacy in Balochistan. THE idea of a durbar still fascinates us and connects us to the subcontinent’s past when kings, rajas, maharajas and nawabs held court. The media, mythology, poetry, theatre, books, and cinema have helped shape the popular image of a ruler seated on his throne, with his ministers and courtiers standing before him. Matters of revenue, war, peace and justice were decided in the ruler’s court. Sometimes, the ruler decided on matters of life and death. However, our fascination may fade once we realise that the legacy of the durbar continues under different names. Pakistan is not the only country carrying this legacy. Many Western countries, including our former colonial ruler, Britain, still retain their monarchies though stripping them of their powers. During the colonial period, the British not only preserved but also strengthened the durbars to control the population and govern indirectly. At the end of British rule, the subcontinent contained approximately 565 princely states. However, historical estimates vary depending on how smaller states are classified. Thirteen were eventually incorporated into Pakistan after their rulers signed Instruments of Accession. Among the courts inherited by Pakistan, none carried greater political symbolism in Balochistan than the Sibi Durbar. It is associated with bitter memories from both the colonial and postcolonial periods. The Sibi Durbar became a major instrument of colonial administrator Robert Sandeman’s frontier policy in the late 19th century. It was an annual winter assembly at which British officials met the officially approved Baloch, Brahui, and Pakhtun chiefs. Tribal disputes were heard, successions and political relationships were considered, honours and allowances were distributed, and the hierarchy created by colonial rule was publicly displayed. Dismantling an institution isn’t the same as changing the political culture that sustained it. Many stories were subsequently associated with the durbar and the British treatment of Baloch and Pakhtun chiefs. One account concerns an earlier Mir Khair Bakhsh Marri, who reportedly refused an order that required the assembled sardars to pull the British political agent’s carriage. According to later accounts, he was punished by being denied privileges granted to more cooperative chiefs. The episode remains part of Baloch political memory. The formal arrangement of the durbar preserved the appearance of the older political order. The chiefs of Sarawan and Jhalawan traditionally sat to the right and left of the Khan of Kalat. Yet the most powerful person in the assembly was not necessarily the Khan. Effective authority rested with the British political agent. Pakistan retained the Sibi Durbar after independence. On Feb 14, 1948, the Quaid addressed what he described as the first “shahi durbar” of Balochistan held under the authority of Pakistan. Speaking to members of the shahi jirga, the sardars and other representatives, he promised political reform. He announced a governor-general’s advisory council as an interim arrangement until a representative constitutional system could be established. One of the last politically consequential Sibi Durbar assemblies took place on Feb 16, 1954. Several sardars submitted a petition to the office of the agent to the governor-general calling for the Balochistan States Union (BSU) to be merged with the former Chief Commissioner’s Province of Balochistan. The BSU emerged from an agreement among the rulers of Kalat, Kharan, Makran, and Lasbela in 1952 and formally came into existence on Oct 3 that year. The four rulers retained limited authority within a union headed initially by the Khan of Kalat. The arrangement, however, survived for only three years. In October 1955, the Union was dissolved and incorporated into the newly created province of West Pakistan under the One Unit scheme. Historians have questioned whether the petition presented at the 1954 durbar represented a spontaneous demand by the sardars or reflected a political process already being encouraged by the central government. Whatever its origins, the episode demonstrated that the durbar could still be used to provide traditional legitimacy for decisions being shaped elsewhere. The abolition of the BSU and the imposition of One Unit deepened political resentment in Balochistan. A few accounts also linked Nawab Nauroz Khan’s uprising with the decision, though his armed struggle began a few years later. The Victoria Memorial Hall, now commonly known as the Jirga Hall, was the principal setting for the Sibi Durbar. It has since been converted into the Sibi Jirga Hall Museum, although it continues to be used for official and cultural functions. Its collection includes photographs, documents, and objects related to the colonial period and the region’s history. Photographs of Jinnah’s 1948 visit preserve the moment when the new state addressed Balochistan through a political institution inherited from the Raj. It is understandable that a newly created country confronting immense administrative and security challenges, could not dismantle every princely and colonial structure overnight. Pakistan required several years, and in some cases decades, to integrate the former princely states. But dismantling an institution is not the same as changing the political culture that sustained it. The princely courts disappeared, the colonial officers departed, and the old administrative structures were formally replaced. Yet the concentration of authority, reliance on selected intermediaries, and preference for managed consultation over genuine representation continued to shape relations between the centre and Balochistan. There is an element of the colonial legacy in Balochistan’s governance model and in the administration of its resources and politics. The Baloch sardars, despite the abolition of the sardari system in 1976, follow the same order and remain subservient to the power elites; hardly anyone raises a voice, and the reason is obvious: they don’t want to lose power or diminish their relationship with the power elites. Though few satirically associate a new institutional mechanism, called ‘workshop’, with the tradition of the durbar, Balochistan is still suffering. Power elites address their grievances through colonial instruments and have not made an earnest attempt to initiate the nation-building process or remove intermediaries — such as sardars and other cronies — between the state and the masses. Perhaps the power elites know that such a shift would change the entire power dynamic in the province and the country. The writer is a security analyst. Published in Dawn, August 30th, 2026

India’s relevance?. INDIA is the most populous country in the world. With a nominal GDP of $4.15 trillion, it is the sixth-largest economy globally, with a big market share that makes countries want to do business with it. Its expansive territory extends down to the northern tip of the Indian Ocean. Despite this strategic weight, why is India losing proportionate relevance in today’s global geopolitics? Five reasons can be identified. Firstly, for decades, India was a partner of choice for the US in countering China’s rise. Imagining itself as the net security provider for South Asia, India joined the America-led Indo-Pacific Strategy, Quad, I2U2, and IMEC. Beijing sensed well in time that America was encircling China with the help of India, Japan and Australia. It could also see that America continued to stir trouble in the South China Sea and could well choke Chinese exports passing through the Pacific and Indian oceans. Pursuant to Russian President Vladimir Putin’s Greater Eurasia partnership initiative, China is increasingly using three overland northern routes and one sea route through the Arctic Ocean. Adapting quickly, America decided to work with China for “constructive strategic stability”. This was announced during President Donald Trump’s meeting with President Xi Jinping in May 2026. The US also reverted its Indo-Pacific Command back to Pacific Command. India’s salience began to change from a strategic US partner to a commercially relevant country. Secondly, nothing has altered the balance of power in South Asia more profoundly than the events of May 2025 . Encouraged by its blatant aggression against Pakistan in 2016 and 2019, Narendra Modi’s government launched missile strikes against nine targets in Pakistan on May 7, wrongly assuming that Pakistan would not be able to respond. It learned to its surprise that Pakistan not only responded robustly on May 10 but also forced India to seek a ceasefire through the US leadership. When the US president helped secure a ceasefire, India did not have the grace to accept the role the US had played. As a result, it found itself in an uncomfortable situation in which the country it sought to please was unresponsive. Pakistan’s military credentials, on the other hand, were recognised by the world at large. Soon after the confrontation, Saudi Arabia entered into a Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement with Pakistan in September 2025. Earlier this month, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement , making India wonder how and why it lost its strategic space in West Asia. Thirdly, South Asia is the world’s least integrated region. A major factor is that India has unfriendly ties with most of its neighbours. It has also made Saarc dysfunctional lest other South Asian states team up to counterbalance it. Indian policymakers have failed to recognise that India’s global stature and relevance will never be realised unless it can take regional countries along. The May 2025 conflict has altered the balance of power in South Asia. Fourthly, for some time, India has tried to project itself as a champion of the Global South. The reality is that China is miles ahead in cultivating developing countries through massive investment in infrastructure, energy and other projects. Furthermore, India has sought to lean closer to the US, clearly signalling its priorities to the Global South. For instance, India opposed the creation of a common BRICS currency to challenge the US dollar, though it does not reject bilateral trade in national currencies. Finally, it was Pakistan, and not India, that was deemed a credible mediator to bring about a ceasefire to the 40-day war between the US and Iran. Pakistan hosted the US and Iran in Islamabad for direct talks, helped conclude the Islamabad MoU, and is continuing its efforts to achieve peace in West Asia. Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts have been appreciated by the entire world except India and Israel that have been courting each other. Three days before the US-Iran war started, the Indian prime minister was in Israel praising the latter as the fatherland without saying a word about the Israeli genocide in Gaza. India’s real priorities stood exposed to Iran and the Gulf countries. Importantly, Pakistan’s rising diplomatic profile has also thwarted India’s decade-long effort to isolate it. While these five reasons have made India strategically less relevant today, Pakistan’s diplomatic and military profile has continued to rise. For Pakistan to sustain its global relevance, an equal effort is needed to build up its economic profile. Given the close linkages between a country’s citizen-centric governance and economic output, the recent debate over how to devolve resources to the grassroots is timely. It should be taken to its logical conclusion. The writer is the chairman of Sanober Institute and a former foreign secretary of Pakistan. Published in Dawn, August 30th, 2026

PTA tells telcos to enforce uniform SIM policy. ISLAMABAD: The telecom sector regulator has directed all three telcos to implement a uniform policy on SIM expiry and recharge amounts, after finding that two telcos were not complying with the prescribed terms and conditions. A senior Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) official said consumers had lodged complaints against Zong and Telenor Pakistan, which has now been acquired by PTCL. The complainants had demanded that prepaid balance should remain valid for the entire active life of the SIM. “The complaints were that these two companies demanded that consumers maintain a certain amount of balance even during the active period of the SIMs, failing which the SIMs were eventually cancelled. The other issue was that they did not carry over the balance amount after the next recharge,” the official added. Zong and the merged company, Ufone/Telenor, did not respond to the query; however, a Jazz official said the active base of a SIM is 90 days, with 180 days as a quarantine period. Orders companies to implement 180-day minimum balance validity policy “After that, the recycling of the SIM is allowed — that means the ownership of the SIM can be changed,” the official added. The official added that Jazz has a recycling policy under which any SIM that remains dormant for up to 720 days is recycled. “But after this period, a dormant SIM is allowed to be totally recycled, and the previous owner can no longer claim any rights over the recycled SIM,” the official added. The determination issued by the PTA directed all telcos to implement a minimum validity period of 180 days for any recharge/balance amount. The PTA has said any expired balance will automatically be reinstated and become usable upon a subsequent recharge during the active life of the SIM, as per the Telecom Consumers Protection Regulations. Telecom companies will not engage in any unfair commercial practices when implementing this decision, which will take effect on Oct 1. The PTA had received multiple complaints from subscribers regarding the forfeiture of unused prepaid balances upon expiry of validity periods. The complainants had said that such deduction and non-adjustment of the balance to subsequent recharges required intervention by the regulator. The complaint lodged with the PTA was that the non-adjustment of the remaining balance significantly impacts the average subscriber financially, particularly low-income subscribers. The PTA has noted that around 97 per cent of subscribers in Pakistan, Azad Jammu and Kashmir, and Gilgit-Baltistan are prepaid users. Published in Dawn, August 30th, 2026

Electric vehicle shift lags amid infrastructure gaps. • PM’s 30pc target stalls as OMCs expand outlets without chargers • Petrol demand stays robust on two-wheeler boom KARACHI: The government is considering several options to reduce the fuel import bill, the latest being the upgrade of refineries at an estimated cost of $6 billion. Earlier efforts to reduce petrol imports by promoting compressed natural gas (CNG) in the automotive sector faltered due to gas shortages. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has called for a 30 per cent shift to electric vehicles within five years to save $4.5bn annually on fuel imports. The initiative, however, is moving slowly due to inadequate infrastructure and a lack of charging stations. Meanwhile, oil marketing companies (OMCs) remain focused on expanding retail fuel outlets, with limited investment in EV charging facilities. Amid rising petrol and diesel prices following the Middle East crisis that began on Feb 28, consumers are gradually shifting to electrified vehicles, including hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs), range-extended electric vehicles (REEVs) and pure battery EVs. Financial statements of OMCs reflect continued retail expansion but little progress on charging infrastructure. Wafi Energy Pakistan Ltd (WEPL), in its half-year results to June 30, reported adding 38 new Shell retail sites, 18 Select stores, two EV recharge facilities and upgrading eight existing sites. It also inaugurated a 7.4-million-litre motor gasoline storage tank at its Tarru Jabba terminal in Nowshera, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, to improve storage and supply resilience. The company plans to expand its Shell retail network further across northern Pakistan. Pakistan State Oil (PSO) reported in its 9MFY26 report that it had deployed nine EV charging stations along the Karachi-to-Peshawar corridor. In its 1HFY26 report, it said its retail network had grown to 3,638 outlets nationwide after adding 107 outlets in FY25. Attock Petroleum Ltd (APL), in the nine months to March 31, commissioned 33 new outlets, taking its network to 811. It is also expanding EV charging and on-grid solar installations at selected outlets and terminals, and progressing DC fast-charging infrastructure with Hubco Green and Huawei. Industry stakeholders say petrol demand will remain robust as 60-65pc of two-wheelers run on petrol, and assembly of such vehicles continues to rise despite higher prices. Pakistan assembled 2.416m two-wheelers in FY26, up from 1.692m in FY25. “EVs will penetrate slowly and may replace petrol in the next five to six years,” a refinery official said, adding that demand destruction in the four-wheeler segment remains marginal. An oil industry executive said about 70pc of petrol, or 5.5m tonnes, is imported annually, while local production is 2.5m tonnes. He noted that globally, EV charging stations are located near shopping malls and residential areas, and many vehicle owners have home chargers. In Pakistan, however, the government is pressing OMCs to install chargers at fuel stations. EV charging also takes considerably longer than refuelling, and fast chargers at stations require high-capacity transformers, which increase costs due to higher power consumption. “Hybrid vehicles are a better option than pure battery vehicles under current circumstances,” he said. There are 4.5m petrol-driven vehicles, including decades-old models, still on the roads. The country, however, needs refinery upgradation to replace ageing plants and remain competitive. Upgradation could also raise annual petrol and diesel output by one million tonnes and is vital for energy security. All five refineries have informed Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik that they are ready to sign modernisation agreements to begin producing Euro-5-compliant fuel locally. The move aims to lower petrol and diesel import bills and prices, improve product quality and efficiency, strengthen domestic supply resilience and advance energy security objectives. The agreement with the government is likely to be signed next month. Successive governments had earlier promoted CNG for automobiles to cut petrol imports, but the plan could not be fully implemented due to gas shortages, resulting in losses for CNG station investors and car owners who bought expensive cylinders and kits. Published in Dawn, August 30th, 2026

‘Disproportionate use of force deepened polarisation in AJK’. LAHORE: The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP) has attributed the recent unrest in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) to longstanding political and socioeconomic grievances, institutional distrust and governance deficits, saying an increasingly confrontational state response, including the disproportionate use of force, further deepened polarisation and eroded public trust. The HRCP fact-finding report, Civic Spaces under Strain in Azad Jammu and Kashmir, (a copy available with Dawn ), stated that the dispute over implementation of a 2025 agreement with the Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), coupled with controversy over 12 seats reserved for Kashmiri refugees in Pakistan, had become central to the political confrontation. The report said negotiations between the government and JAAC failed on May 30, after which the government proscribed the organisation on June 5 under the AJK Anti-Terrorism Act 2014 and imposed restrictions on movement and communications, including a prolonged suspension of mobile internet services. The ensuing unrest coincided with the AJK Legislative Assembly elections, which were eventually held in phases because of security concerns. The HRCP mission, which conducted fact-finding and election observation from Aug 8 to 10 after a stakeholder consultation in Islamabad on July 31, said it received sharply conflicting accounts about the scale of violence, JAAC’s methods and the conduct of security forces. However, it found broad agreement among political and community stakeholders, including people critical of JAAC, that the underlying dispute should have been resolved through political dialogue rather than coercion. HRCP fact-finding report calls for independent investigation into deaths, injuries during protests The commission expressed particular concern at the allegations of lethal and excessive use of force against protesters. It said the AJK police chief had reported around 38 security personnel killed and 742 police personnel injured since June but the HRCP mission also received multiple accounts from families, alleging that protesters had been killed or seriously injured by the security forces. The HRCP cautioned that it could not independently establish the full scale or circumstances of civilian casualties, particularly because it was unable to access Rawalakot, one of the main centres of violence. It therefore called for an independent and impartial investigation into all deaths and serious injuries since June, including whether the use of force was lawful, necessary and proportionate. The report also raised concerns at the government’s use of anti-terrorism and preventive-detention provisions against political activists. It said at least 147 JAAC activists were initially placed on the Fourth Schedule, while a series of notifications issued between June and August reportedly brought the total number of political workers, journalists, residents and activists listed under anti-terrorism legislation to at least 157. The HRCP urged authorities to ensure due process for everyone arrested in connection with the protests, including their production before courts, access to lawyers and information about the grounds for arrest. It called for independent review of cases against protesters, activists, journalists and political workers, with cases withdrawn where individuals had been detained or prosecuted solely for peaceful political activity or lawful assembly. It also criticised restrictions on journalism and access to information, saying journalists had faced arrests, legal action, restrictions on access to affected areas and special security requirements while the prolonged communications shutdown severely constrained independent reporting and verification of deaths, injuries, arrests and alleged electoral irregularities. The report noted that journalists had reported pressure from both state authorities and JAAC supporters, creating a difficult environment for independent reporting during the unrest and elections. The communications shutdown, according to the mission, went far beyond political activity, disrupting banking, education, commerce, transport, public administration and healthcare. On the elections, the HRCP made a distinction between political boycott and physical obstruction of voters. At polling stations it visited in Bagh, it found limited evidence of systematic physical coercion by JAAC supporters. In some areas, extremely low turnout appeared to reflect voluntary boycott, political disillusionment, fear and the wider security and communications environment rather than voters being physically prevented from casting ballots. At the same time, the mission said the heavy deployment of security personnel, prolonged communications restrictions, boycott by major political actors, phased polling and postponement of seven constituencies raised wider questions about the credibility of the electoral process. The HRCP said the credibility of elections could not be judged solely by what happened inside polling stations but also had to take into account the broader environment in which voters, candidates, political parties, journalists and civil society exercised their rights. The mission observed orderly voting at the polling stations it visited in Bagh. At some other stations, however, polling staff reported exceptionally low turnout and said voters had not been threatened or prevented from voting, attributing the low participation to a voluntary boycott. The HRCP also noted particularly low participation by women, with respondents linking their reluctance to vote partly to the wider climate of insecurity. It said reports concerning violence against women and the placement of women protesters on the Fourth Schedule required independent verification but indicated that the unrest may have generated fear affecting women’s participation. The report concluded that the 2026 electoral process took place amid unresolved political grievances, insecurity, communications restrictions and significant limitations on independent observation. It stopped short of concluding that the elections had been systematically manipulated or that voters had been systematically prevented from participating. Published in Dawn, August 30th, 2026

Nine cops punished for send-off to suspended SHO. SAHIWAL: District Police Officer (DPO) Usman Tipu suspended nine policemen of the Harappa Police Station after they gave Station House Officer (SHO) Majid Ashfaq a warm sendoff and showered him with rose petals after he was suspended from service by the DPO for faulty investigation, receiving bribes and misuse of authority in a sexual assault case. SHO Majid Ashfaq was suspended on Aug 27 but the following day, his colleagues organised a farewell reception in his honour on police station premises. A mobile video of the event went viral, prompting the DPO to take action. “Police are a disciplined and self-accountable force. No one will be allowed to glorify unprofessional attitude or defiance of a superior’s orders through such bizarre actions,” Mr Tipu told Dawn . Those suspended for participating in the reception include Sub Inspector Imran, ASIs Khalid Naeem, Gulzar Ahmed and Nadeem Iqbal, head constables Naeem Khan and Nisar Ahmed and constables Mudasir Liaqat, Mubashir Pervaiz and Muhammad Akhter. It is said only the female constable was spared who did not participate in farewell reception. The suspension order (Dawn has a copy) says, “They (officials) were suspended on account of inefficiency, undisciplined act and unbecoming of a member of a disciplined force”. The case at the centre of the controversy dates back to four years when a woman, a resident of Harappa, was allegedly lured by her former male friend who had previously trapped her during her stay in Lahore with promises of marriage but later blackmailed her with explicit videos. The woman had shifted to Lahore for preparation of her competitive exam. Later, she moved back to Harappa and had an arranged marriage in Chak 56/GD Modain. After her marriage, the suspect continued blackmailing her, extorting Rs1.5m in gold ornaments, Rs40,000 cash and daily expenses for his car. When we prettify the cross. THROUGH UNTRUE Imagine if Jesus had lived in our time, preached inconvenient truths, challenged the powerful, and threatened both religious and political authorities. Imagine if He were executed by electric chair. Would we place electric chairs in our churches instead of crosses? We may cringe at the thought. But perhaps we react that way because we have prettified the Cross so much that we have forgotten what it originally represented. We now wear necklaces with small crosses as pendants. We adorn church altars and our homes with beautifully crafted crosses. There is nothing wrong with honoring the Cross. But there is a danger in prettifying it that we forget what it actually means. The Cross was originally an instrument of torture and execution, much like the electric chair. Crucifixion was a public spectacle of extreme suffering and dehumanization. This helps us understand Peter’s reaction when Jesus predicted that He would be crucified. He took Jesus aside and protested: “God forbid! No such thing shall ever happen to you” (Matthew 16:22). Like many Jews of his time, Peter expected the Messiah to be a powerful king, triumphantly wielding authority from His throne, not a helpless man hanging on a cross. We are not so different from Peter. We adore Christ crucified, but a prettified Cross can become just an ornament, that is beautiful to behold, but demanding little from us. It reflects our preference for a God who gives us everything but asks nothing in return. The philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche criticized Christianity for glorifying weakness and suffering. From his perspective, venerating the Cross could seem like celebrating the plight of those crushed or victimized by human cruelty. But perhaps Nietzsche’s mistake was to assume that power must always express itself through domination and self-will. What if God reveals a different kind of power, a power that does not crush the weak but joins them in their suffering? What if the Cross demonstrates His refusal to abandon us in our darkest moments? On the Cross, Jesus revealed that God does not love us from a distance. He is not indifferent to the pain that afflicts us. He comes close to us and embraces our suffering so that, ultimately, He can overcome it through love. Unbelievers may see only a man hanging on a cross, but we Christians see God hanging there, revealing the depth of His unconditional love for us. The Cross tells us what love looks like when it refuses to surrender, run away, or give up. That is why Jesus’ words in today’s Gospel are addressed not only to His first disciples but to all of us: “Whoever wants to be my disciple must deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me. For whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for me will find it” (Matthew 16:24–25). So, when you look at a cross today, or when you touch the cross hanging around your neck, listen to the uncomfortable questions it asks you: What are you willing to sacrifice for the love of God? And perhaps the most difficult question of all: Can you remain faithful to God when He seems to have abandoned you? On the cross, Jesus cried out, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). Yet He did not turn away from the Father. That is why the cross is not merely a symbol of suffering. It is the ultimate sign of faith that endures when God seems silent and absent. I once presided at the funeral Mass of a man who had achieved much in his lifetime, only to undergo a terrible ordeal because of a terminal illness. In her eulogy, his daughter said: “We have great love and respect for our father. But we admire him most, not for his success and achievements, but for the way he embraced the intolerable pain he had to endure every day. It was when he became most helpless that he showed us what courage truly means. He bravely clung to his faith despite the excruciating pain he had to bear. Perhaps this is the greatest legacy he has left us, his children.”

The paradox of the cross. REFLECTIONS TODAY It is often said that the Christian faith took the whole Mediterranean world by storm; what started as an insignificant “Jesus movement” in Palestine soon became a universal religion that encompassed the whole Roman Empire. St. Luke who narrates the development and spread of Christianity in Acts of the Apostles provides the explanation through a word of caution of Rabbi Gamaliel to the Sanhedrin concerning the intransigent Apostles: “Have nothing to do with these men, and let them go. For if this endeavor or this activity is of human origin, it will destroy itself. But if it comes from God, you will not be able to destroy them; you may even find yourselves fighting against God” (Acts 5:38-39). That finally Paul the Apostle arrives in Rome, in chains and yet free to preach the Gospel, proves this: the nascent faith-movement comes from God and human beings cannot destroy it. Being of divine origin does not mean, however, that Christianity triumphed mightily over the ancient religions like Gideon dispersing the Midianite army with blowing of horns and breaking of jars (Jgs 7:20) or Joshua causing the walls of Jericho to collapse with a seven-day march around the city (Jos 6:4). Christianity conquered the hearts of peoples with what St. Paul calls “the message of the cross”—foolishness to the pagans and a stumbling block to Jews, but to the believers, the power and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:22-24). In today’s Gospel, Simon Peter is shocked to hear Jesus predicting that he will suffer and die in Jerusalem. And rightly so! He had just confessed Jesus as the Messiah of God, and Jesus had called him “Rock” because of that confession. How, then, can Jesus speak of the cross when a crucified man is cursed by God! The Messiah was thought to be a glorious figure, not a man of suffering! The message is just as shocking when preached to the Gentile world. A crucified Messiah as God’s means of reconciling a lost world was a bizarre message, not “good news.” In the early third century, the pagan Caecilius Natalis said of the Christians, “I hear that they adore the head of an ass, the basest of creatures—a most worthy and appropriate religion for such manners.” A graffito of a man’s body with an ass’s head found in Palestine reflects a similar response by Gentiles to the “folly of the cross.” Under this graffito was the caption: “Alexamenos worships [his] God.” The cross can only be “good news” if its meaning is completely overturned. This was shown in the resurrection of Jesus. God was pleased with the obedience “unto death, unto the cross” of Jesus that he raised him from the dead. St. Paul, the first theologian, was a theologian of the cross. According to him, the cross is the initiative of God and the demonstration of his great love: “God proves his love for us in that while we were still sinners Christ died for us” (Rom 5:8). Jesus’ cross is not an accident of history but a historical witness of God’s unmerited love and saving grace: God was reconciling the world to himself through Christ (cf 2 Cor 5:19). Paul came to this realization not as an afterthought but through a dramatic encounter with the risen Christ. On the way to Damascus, Christ “apprehended” him and showed him that he is in fact what the disciples preached him to be. Paul was struck by the “power and glory of the cross” as if by lightning. This was the conviction that he then preached to both Jews and Gentiles. They understood the paradox of the cross and became believers, ready to lose their lives that they might find it in Jesus. First Reading • Jer 20:7-9 You duped me, O Lord, and I let myself be duped; you were too strong for me, and you triumphed. All the day I am an object of laughter; everyone mocks me. Whenever I speak, I must cry out, violence and outrage is my message; the word of the Lord has brought me derision and reproach all the day. I say to myself, I will not mention him, I will speak in his name no more. But then it becomes like fire burning in my heart, imprisoned in my bones; I grow weary holding it in, I cannot endure it.
