Mass transport that works: Fulfilling the promise of the EDSA Busway. ENDEAVOR During the Covid-19 pandemic, the Department of Transportation (DOTr) led by then Secretary Arthur “Art” Tugade took the initiative of launching the EDSA Busway or EDSA Carousel project in June 2020 to ease the daily commute problems of tens of thousands of Filipinos. Within a month, a dedicated median us lane adjacent to the MRT-3 line had been installed. Moreover, the DOTr rationalized the operations of public utility buses. Sixty-one fragmented feeder routes were replaced with a single, streamlined Carousel route running from Monumento in Caloocan down to the Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange (PITX). Concrete barriers were installed for physical segregation from general traffic and special buses with left-facing doors were introduced. A public-private partnership agreement was forged with the SM Group to build elevated median stations and pedestrian concourses. These structures directly link major commercial hubs to the inner-lane EDSA Carousel stations, namely: SM North EDSA in Quezon City; SM Megamall (Mandaluyong and Ortigas); and SM Mall of Asia in Pasay City. The SM Group donated commercial spaces and assumed full funding for the construction of three major state-of-the-art concourses in the three mall sites. Under the agreement, SM secured the rights to name the stations, administer, maintain, and manage the facilities based on DOTr guidelines. This arrangement ensured long-term, high-quality upkeep and security for the pedestrian hubs The concourses were designed based on the conceptual framework of urban transport reform advocate Eduardo Yap. Despite policy support, advocacy groups like the Move as One Coalition have flagged zero funding allocated specifically for the EDSA Busway under the DOTr's proposed 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP). The DOTr defends this fiscal shift by leaning into the aforementioned public-private partnership (PPP) model to sustain future upgrades while keeping current systems rolling. Recall that the EDSA Busway emerged as a model implementation of the Public-Private Partnership (PPP) framework established by the PPP Center under the stewardship of Cosette Canilao during the Aquino administration. Ms. Canilao has since joined Aboitiz InfraCapital, the infrastructure investment arm of the Aboitiz Group, as President and CEO. For the sake of long-term infrastructure development, it is imperative to adopt a proactive and decisive stance in implementing the Public-Private Partnership (PPP) template. The executive branch must demonstrate its political will in completing priority infrastructure projects like the EDSA Busway. Prolonged pauses will be detrimental rather than helpful, as time is ticking away. There are only less than two years before the expiry of the current administration’s watch and it stands to reason that it would like to be remembered as a regime that responded to urgent concerns of the citizenry just like the easing of mobility throughout the EDSA corridor. High hopes were ignited when Vince Dizon was appointed as transportation secretary, but his stint was short-lived. Even before completing nine months at its helm, he was called to take over the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) to stem the tide of the public outrage over ghost flood control projects. The EDSA Busway has already demonstrated a simple but powerful truth. When government gives priority to public transportation, millions of commuters stand to benefit. What began as an emergency response to the pandemic has evolved into a vital component of Metro Manila’s mass transport system. The challenge now is to finish what has been started and to do it expeditiously. SM Prime Holdings’ commitment to complete three major EDSA Busway stations should be welcomed as an example of the efficacy of the PPP approach. Properly designed and completed, they will make the Busway a showcase of safer, more accessible and more convenient commuting, particularly for senior citizens, persons with disabilities, women, children and daily commuters bearing the brunt of long journeys that take many hours to complete, thereby sapping huge stores of energy and reducing quality time for families. Government must move with dispatch and determination, establishing clear timelines for completion and operationalization. When a public transport solution works, government should not allow it to languish. It should make it better, expand its reach and finish the job. Once completed, the EDSA Busway will demonstrate with clarity that government is capable of bringing to full fruition effective solutions that give to the people what they have always longed to attain: safe and dignified travel and a better quality of daily life.

A week of initialisms and acronyms. While most will refer to both categories as acronyms; initialisms are read letter by letter, while acronyms are a short word made from the letters of a long group of words. For today’s column, the initialisms would be DTI for Department of Trade and Industry, and AI for Artificial Intelligence; while the acronym for Artist Atelier Philippines, would be the newly coined ARTa. Here are two launch events I recently had the pleasure of attending. The DTI AI and Scale Up Center - Our Department of Trade and Industry, in partnership with Converge ICT Solutions, launched the DTI AI and Scale Up Center at their Gil Puyat office. It’s a practical hub for technology adoption and potential business growth. At its core, it’s a hands on resource facility; that allows companies, start-ups, and local SMEs to learn how to integrate AI and digital tools into their operations. Backed by the Tatak Pinoy Strategy, the Philippine Innovation Act, and the Innovative Start Up Act, I really appreciated the intent of what was being officially opened that afternoon. It’s no longer just words on official documents or lofty aims of an existing Strategy and Acts; but the realization of that intent, and establishing concrete avenues to achieve those goals. Too often, we speak of Philippine businesses not being competitive in the global market, or that we lag behind in incorporating technology, or that we find scaling up to be too formidable a task. Here then was the DTI taking the proverbial bull by the horns, and creating a solution-based pathway. As DTI Secretary Cristina Roque was proud to say, “This AI and Scale Up Center provides a realistic, accessible entry point for Filipino businesses to explore and adapt modern technology like AI. Scaling a business requires usable tools and expert guidance, so that innovative ideas can turn into functional solutions. By bringing technology leaders like Converge together with our local enterprises, we are giving businesses of all sizes the practical knowledge and connectivity they need to improve efficiency, and stay competitive.” From Practical Workshops, to technical consultations, and scaling programs; Converge is ready to be that ideal partner in making these all available to our SMEs. As Converge founder and CEO Dennis Uy remarked, “We are proud to partner with DTI in helping local businesses take realistic steps toward digital transformation. Through reliable connectivity and hands on technology solutions, our goal is to help companies understand AI, streamline their operations, and expand their reach in today’s evolving market.” With the array of DTI’s private sector partners who were on hand to show their support; the know how, technical expertise, and best practices learned by other established local businesses will be made available for our SMEs to learn from, as made accessible and powered by Converge. I salute this partnership, and the Center that has been created; and can only hope that SMEs will appreciate the great opportunity being offered, and how it’s a ‘helping hand’ that can go a very long way. ARTa, the Artist Atelier Philippines - There’s a new Creative Learning Center that’s located at the Kirov Tower, Proscenium, Rockwell Center, Makati; and it’s the brainchild of noted businesswoman and artist Elena Coyiuto. For those familiar with Elena and her IG handle madameinshades, they’ll acknowledge that her readiness to support worthy causes is matched by her vitality and dedication to the Arts. Having mounted solo exhibits of her own paintings, it would only be a logical extension to want to share the wonders of this mid-life shift; and offer it to others who may also be yearning to express themselves in a medium they have had no training for. And that’s precisely what the Artist Atelier Philippines (ARTa) hopes to provide. In the atelier’s curriculum are visual and literary arts programs for beginners, for hobbyists, and the aspiring artist. It’s guided instruction that may help answer one’s perpetual wondering if there was some form of artistic expression that one can rekindle or simply ignite. It’s the “What If…” being given that window of opportunity to become a reality. It may be what Elena herself faced at one point in her journey; and she’s evidently saying that if one needs help in navigating, she’s offering a wonderful option. From Drawing, to Acrylic Painting, Watercolor, Creative Writing, and even such specialized subjects as Floral Arranging, and Weaving, ARTa is offering basic and intermediate programs. No portfolio required, the courses are accessible to all. One can even arrange for private group sessions, and corporate workshops. Elena Coyiuto remarked, “ARTa is my advocacy in sharing the love of art and making creativity accessible to everyone. I hope to inspire people of all ages and skill levels to explore their creativity and discover art as a lifelong source of expression, connection, and personal growth.” Head to the ARTa Philippines website, or check their IG and FB pages.

Lubao flooding exposes urgent need for better flood control. A two-storey house being swallowed by a raging river should never be dismissed as just another dramatic video content. But that was precisely what happened in Barangay Sta. Rita-Sto. Cristo, Lubao, Pampanga, on Aug. 28. As floodwaters surged, the riverbank gave way and a home was swept into the torrent and then swallowed by the rampaging floodwater in a matter of minutes. The terrifying and heart-wrenching scene is a warning—and an indictment of how dangerously unprepared communities remain for extreme flooding. The timing could hardly be more ominous. On Aug. 29, PAGASA placed Pampanga and neighboring provinces under a red rainfall warning as the southwest monsoon, or habagat, continued to dump heavy rain over parts of Luzon. A red warning means serious flooding is expected in flood-prone areas. The Sta. Rita Dam incident exposes a problem far bigger than one overwhelmed structure. The National Irrigation Administration said a huge volume of water rushed downstream and overwhelmed the dam, while debris from forests and agricultural areas accumulated and clogged some of its gates. The resulting surge damaged portions of the slope protection and retaining wall. That demands accountability. But accountability must be comprehensive. The government must answer for whether dams, dikes, drainage systems, and flood-control structures are properly designed, maintained, inspected and upgraded. It must explain whether danger zones are being enforced and why residential structures continue to exist along vulnerable riverbanks and dikes. But the government is not the only actor responsible. Illegal logging and destructive land-clearing practices, including kaingin in vulnerable upland areas, must be confronted because denuded watersheds can worsen erosion and send enormous amounts of debris downstream. If investigations establish that illegally cut timber or other improperly managed upland debris contributed to the obstruction at Sta. Rita, those responsible must be held accountable. Residents, too, must face the truth, unforgettable as it may be: Like them, a river needs space to avoid swelling. Building houses on dikes, easements, and riverbanks may appear harmless when the river is calm. During extreme rainfall, however, such structures can endanger lives—and serve as obstacles that complicate flood management and evacuation. The answer is not another round of promises after disaster strikes. The government must pursue integrated flood mitigation: Rehabilitate watersheds, enforce river easements, clear waterways and drainage channels before the rainy season, modernize dams and dikes, strengthen flood forecasting and early-warning systems, and conduct regular independent safety audits of critical infrastructure. Flood-control projects must also be transparent, scientifically designed, and subjected to public scrutiny. The private sector must do its share. Developers must respect hazard maps and no-build zones. Industries must prevent waste and debris from entering waterways. Companies can finance watershed rehabilitation, river cleanup, community early-warning systems and disaster-preparedness programs—not merely distribute relief goods after floods. And every Filipino has a responsibility. Do not dump garbage into waterways. Do not build illegally on riverbanks and dikes. Report illegal logging, destructive land clearing, and unsafe construction. Heed evacuation orders. Participate in community disaster-preparedness efforts. Most importantly, demand accountability for every peso spent on flood-control infrastructure. Climate and extreme weather may be beyond anyone’s control. But negligence is not. The house swept away in Lubao should therefore become a national lesson. Flooding is not simply a natural disaster. Its consequences are shaped by decisions made in government offices, boardrooms, forests, farms, construction sites, and communities. The Lubao river has delivered its warning. Now the country must decide whether to listen, or wait for the next structure to disappear.

Cooperatives seek 10-fold tax exemption increase to ₱100 million. The Philippine Chamber of Cooperatives, Inc. (Coop Chamber) is asking Congress to raise the reserve fund tax-exemption ceiling for cooperatives to ₱100 million from the current ₱10 million. Coop Chamber Secretary General Edwin A. Bustillos told reporters that the proposal is a long-overdue update to a four-decade-old threshold, one that will not hurt government coffers. During technical working group discussions, Bustillos revealed the proposal faced pushback from the Department of Finance (DOF) and the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) over potential revenue losses. However, Bustillos explained that the ₱10 million threshold was instituted nearly 40 years ago when the sector was significantly smaller. He noted that surplus funds generated by cooperatives are legally earmarked as statutory reserves for social development rather than commercial profits. “Cooperatives’ surplus goes back to the people. They have statutory funds that are channeled to the community,” Bustillos said. For instance, roughly ₱3 billion has been injected into community development funds for infrastructure, scholarships, and medical missions, among other initiatives. Bustillos added that spending on community development, education, and training goes uncounted in gross domestic product (GDP), despite cooperatives pumping billions into these efforts. The sector also shoulders the cost of leadership training, financial inclusion, and financial literacy programs that would otherwise rely on government agency partnerships. Furthermore, he stressed that trillions of pesos circulating within the sector help nearly 14 million members start and sustain small businesses, pursue their education, and cover medical bills for family members. Citing these on-the-ground contributions, the Coop chamber argued that while granting a higher tax relief threshold means forgone tax revenues, those funds ultimately recirculate into local communities. “Therefore, raising the accumulated reserves threshold to ₱100 million would not result in a significant revenue loss for the BIR and the DOF,” Bustillos said. “Hopefully, the ₱100-million cap will be passed during the Senate’s second regular session.” Under the Philippine Cooperative Code, registered cooperatives transacting exclusively with members are exempt from national and local internal revenue taxes. Transactions with non-members, however, remain subject to applicable taxes. Cooperatives with accumulated reserves and undivided net savings of up to ₱10 million enjoy comprehensive tax privileges. Those exceeding the threshold pay taxes on the excess, though they retain specific exemptions for local taxes and qualified transactions. Bustillos pointed to this framework to clarify that “billionaire” cooperatives still contribute to government revenues by paying taxes on non-member transactions and reserves above the threshold. Only about 140 of the roughly 20,000 cooperatives in the country fall into the “billionaire” category—mostly in finance, with a few in agriculture. Tax privileges apply only to core activities outlined in their articles of cooperation, bylaws, and BIR tax exemption certificates, leaving all other economic activities taxable. Beyond tax disputes, the sector is grappling with digital compliance challenges. The Coop Chamber noted that many micro-cooperatives—particularly those representing farmers, fisherfolk, and indigenous peoples—struggle to meet digitized reporting mandates due to a lack of devices and reliable internet access. To address this, Coop Chamber Chairperson Noel D. Raboy said the group is pushing for compliance relief similar to that offered by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), such as permitting simple bookkeeping instead of requiring costly certified tax accountants (CTAs) for small co-ops. These ongoing struggles have driven the sector to seek systemic legislative reform. The Coop Chamber plans to consolidate its members into a unified “co-op vote” and field a senatorial candidate under a national cooperative party in the 2028 elections. By placing a cooperative leader in the Senate, the sector aims to champion community-based development and secure lasting policy support for micro-enterprises.

JuanHand pushes ₱1-trillion lending spree as bank credit slows down. Digital cash lender JuanHand is poised to extend more loans beyond the ₱1.16 trillion it has disbursed to date, with a new product allowing borrowers to take out additional funds within their credit limit without first settling their existing loan. JuanHand has introduced its top-up loan, allowing eligible users to apply for additional funds even while they have an existing loan, with approvals taking as little as five minutes through its operator, WeFund Lending Corp.’s AI-powered tool. “Through the utilization of WeFund’s proprietary AI, the platform can analyze user data and provide approval in as fast as 5 minutes,” JuanHand said. JuanHand is the Philippine subsidiary of New York Stock Exchange-listed global financial technology firm FinVolution Group. To date, JuanHand has extended over ₱1.16 trillion in loans to more than 20 million Filipinos. According to the digital lender, the new top-up loan feature is designed to offer borrowers another option “when they need access to additional financial resources, provided that the new loan remains within their available credit limit and applicable eligibility requirements.” Under its current terms, borrowers can apply for loans of up to ₱50,000, with daily interest rates set as low as 0.025 percent, “subject to applicable loan terms and eligibility.” This feature has veered away from conventional digital micro-lending models. “Rather than limiting borrowers to a single borrowing experience, this allows eligible users to borrow again as long as it is within their credit limit,” JuanHand explained. JuanHand has simplified its requirements, making the application process accessible by requiring “only a registered mobile number and one valid ID” before the AI-driven underwriting evaluates the borrower’s profile. This development comes alongside Filipinos’ growing reliance on e-wallets, digital lenders, and digital banks. Digital lending has become crucial for expanding financial services beyond traditional banking networks, the firm noted. “As digital borrowing continues to evolve, JuanHand remains focused on serving underserved yet creditworthy Filipinos” while responding to the changing needs of local consumers. Credit products such as JuanHand’s could offer some thrust the overall financial system needs, as it has seen moderating lending activity in June. Lending by big banks in the Philippines grew by 9.8 percent in June, its slowest pace in four months, as borrowers turned more cautious, dampening demand for loans. It slumped from the peak of 12.1 percent in May. Outstanding loans stood at ₱17.33 trillion as of end-June, according to the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP). (Derco Rosal)

First Lady thanks late Marcos aide-de-camp for ‘courage, loyalty and dedication’. First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos has paid tribute to Maj. Ma. Joshua Santiago, thanking the late soldier for the “courage, loyalty and dedication” with which he served by President Marcos’ side. In an Instagram post late Saturday, Aug. 29, Araneta-Marcos extended her condolences to Santiago’s family, particularly his wife, Argel, and their children, Army and Navy. “A heartfelt thank you to Major Joshua Santiago for the courage, loyalty and dedication with which he served by my husband’s side,” the First Lady said. She said the family was in their thoughts and prayers, and assured them that Santiago was deeply valued by those who had the privilege of knowing and serving alongside him. “May you find comfort in knowing how deeply Jam was valued, and how much his service, friendship and presence meant to all who had the privilege of knowing and serving alongside him,” she said. Araneta-Marcos, who visited the wake at the Libingan ng mga Bayani on Aug. 28, also thanked Santiago for his dedication to duty, saying his service would always be remembered with “respect, gratitude and affection.” Santiago served as Marcos’ aide-de-camp, a military officer assigned to assist a senior official by handling official engagements, coordinating activities, and providing close support in carrying out the official’s duties. President Marcos earlier mourned Santiago in a Facebook post, describing him as “a soldier of courage, an officer I could depend on and, above all, a good man.” The President also visited Santiago’s wake at the Libingan ng mga Bayani in Taguig City on Aug. 27, where he was seen expressing his condolences to the family, particularly to Argel. The video of Marcos’ visit was muted, with only piano music playing, so his conversation with the family was inaudible. Neither Marcos nor the First Lady mentioned the cause of Santiago’s death.

Alan Cayetano wants more details on 2026 spending, gov’t debt as Senate tackles 2027 budget. As the Senate starts deliberations on the 2027 national budget, Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano urged the government’s economic team to show how much of the 2026 budget has been spent, where the funds went, and how much the country has borrowed. In a letter to Senate Finance Committee chief Sen. Joseph Victor “JV” Ejercito, Cayetano raised these questions, saying the information would help senators study the proposed budget and ensure that the budget process is transparent and “faithful to the priorities they all promised to serve.” “There is no measure this Congress passes each year that is more consequential and touches more Filipino lives than the General Appropriations Act (GAA),” Cayetano said in his letter. “It is our values and priorities written in numbers. That is why we owe it to our people to get this budget right,” he emphasized. Earlier, Ejercito kicked off the hearings on the P7.2-trillion national budget during the Development Budget Coordination Committee (DBCC) briefing on Thursday, August 27. Prior to this, Cayetano, in his letter, asked the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) how much of the 2026 budget had been released, committed to projects, and actually paid out. The senator also called on the DBM to provide each department’s and agency’s absorptive capacity — that is, how much each can realistically spend. Cayetano also asked whether funds under the government’s Unified Package for Livelihoods, Industry, Food, and Transport (UPLIFT) framework had reached the intended initiatives, and requested details on their release and use. The lawmaker also sought details on the national government’s total debt as of July 31, 2026, as well as the loans and bonds it took out or guaranteed over the past three years. He also asked which foreign loans and grants were still awaiting government approval. Cayetano also requested a list of funds that had been transferred, realigned, or added to other programs since July 2023, including where the money came from and where it went. He urged the agencies to submit their answers and supporting documents early to provide senators sufficient time to review them ahead of the agency budget hearings. At the same time, the Minority Leader also assured the Senate Majority bloc of his “full and good faith cooperation” in crafting “the best possible budget for 2027.” “(It must be) a budget that honors God, builds communities, and transforms the nation,” he said of the proposed 2027 national budget.

First Lady bids farewell to outgoing Japanese envoy Endo. First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos held a final catch-up with outgoing Japanese Ambassador to the Philippines Endo Kazuya and his wife Akiko at her office in Manila, as the couple prepares to wrap up their two-and-a-half-year stay in the country. In an Instagram post on Saturday evening, Aug. 29, Araneta-Marcos thanked the Endos for their friendship and the memories they made during their stay, saying the Philippines would always be a "second home" to them. "One last catch-up with Ambassador Endo Kazuya and Madame Endo before they wrap up their stay in the Philippines," the First Lady said. "Thank you for the friendship, warmth and wonderful memories over the past two and a half years," she added. The meeting, held in her office at the PMS Building on Aug. 27, featured a light conversation among the three, with the First Lady and the couple seen smiling and laughing in a video posted alongside her message. The Endos gave Araneta-Marcos a blue Uniqlo polo shirt bearing the embroidered logo of the 70th anniversary of the Philippines-Japan Friendship Anniversary on the left breast. The First Lady, meanwhile, gave the couple a copy of "Philippine First Ladies Portraits," written by José "Pepe" Rodríguez and painted by artist Lulu "Coching" Rodríguez. Other keepsakes symbolizing the Philippines were also featured, including a framed map and images depicting traditional Filipino dances such as singkil, tinikling, and cariñosa. In a Facebook post, Araneta-Marcos said they looked back on the "many special memories" the couple made in the Philippines and, more importantly, the friendships they formed during their stay. "Thank you both for your warmth, kindness and friendship — and, of course, for the thoughtful gifts!" she said. “I hope our little keepsakes will always remind you that you have a second home here and many friends who will be happy to welcome you back,” she added. The farewell came a day after President Marcos honored Endo during a farewell call at Malacañang, conferring on him the Order of Sikatuna, Grand Cross with Distinction, for his contributions to strengthening Philippine-Japan relations. Endo was recognized for promoting bilateral exchanges and deepening cooperation in defense, security, and development cooperation, as well as supporting Philippine priorities in infrastructure, education, transportation, maritime domain awareness, and human resource development. The Presidential Communications Office also cited his efforts to advance Japan's longstanding commitment to peace and development in Mindanao, including support for the peace process, grassroots development, and the transition of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao. Endo, who thanked Filipinos in an Aug. 28 social media post as he ended his tour of duty, described his two-and-a-half years in the Philippines as "truly unforgettable" and said he was humbled to have served as ambassador "at the height of our two countries’ partnership."

Going nuts over coco: Discover the Filipino brands reinventing the humble coconut. More than just a fruit, the coconut is deeply woven into the fabric of daily Filipino life. Long revered as the country’s “Tree of Life,” its bark, trunk, leaves, and roots flavor local cuisine, supply materials for artisanal crafts, and stand today as crucial building blocks in our push toward sustainability and economic growth. In the Philippines, there is no such thing as “too much” coconut, as local entrepreneurs and creators continue to push the boundaries of what this tree can offer. Reaching beyond food and beverage into beauty, wellness, home essentials, and other sustainable materials, the coconut evolution is proudly showcased at the COCONUTPhilippines Trade Fair 2026. Convened at the SMX Convention Center in Pasay City, the COCONUTPhilippines Trade Fair 2026, running from Aug. 26 to 30, is the country’s biggest fair yet of the coconut’s modern potential. Featuring over 300 MSMEs, the trade fair was organized by the DTI's Bureau of Market Development, Promotions, and OTOP (DTI-BMDPO), in partnership with the Philippine Coconut Authority (PCA), to empower local enterprises and expand their market reach. Redefining the Filipino pantry The SMX Convention Center halls overflowed with unexpected coconut food innovations. While Filipinos have long loved coconut in everything from savory dishes to desserts, it is now making its way onto dining tables as a daily condiment and essential staple. While coconut vinegar has been around for a while, coconut-based soy sauce and seasonings have featured prominently as amino acid-rich, slightly sweet alternatives to traditional soy sauce. Quezon Province’s Yakap at Halik (YK) Multi-Purpose Cooperative showcased coconut catsup. A blend of coconut milk, water, and vinegar with a milder flavor, perfect for fried and grilled dishes. Marketing staff Teodora O. Glorioso noted DTI’s help in securing certifications to overcome nationwide expansion hurdles. Coming in hot, MSMEs introduced coconut hot sauces: Hot Heads featured a rich coconut cream sauce infused with habanero, while Quezon’s Best offered a fiery blend from premium chilis. Finally, The Power of Slow introduced a fresh twist on coconut beverages with a sap-based energy drink. Supporting farmers and wellness, the brand is established overseas, but head of customer development RJ Samson highlighted local adoption challenges, which DTI is actively addressing through trade fairs and mall pop-ups. Sustainable fashion Beyond the kitchen, coconut is also making its mark in Filipino fashion. From Zamboanga, Agricooltourist De La Paz (AGL Collection) turns coconut fibers and husks into sturdy yet stylish handbags, an initiative born from the desire to support local farmers, many of whom are also the backbone of their production. The brand also showcased prototype lamps crafted from the same materials, effectively upcycling agricultural waste from the coconut fruit into functional home décor. But turning farmers into artisans came with its own hurdles. With limited exposure to the market, the team leaned heavily on DTI for guidance, from labeling and branding to training and seminars covering both handicraft techniques and financial literacy. With that, Ronnel Barbon, marketing staff, says the brand's next goal is steady growth, securing consistent orders and continuing to refine its products for a wider, more discerning market. Shells to clean energy Redefining clean-burning fuel, CG’s Coconut Charcoal Trading of Bohol repurposes discarded coconut shells into charcoal briquettes. John Mark Baldo, who manages the business operations, shared that the family business stemmed from an unusual romance between his grandparents. What started decades ago as a grandfather's gesture to win over his bride has now grown into an enterprise that manufactures and exports coconut charcoal briquettes to Japan, China, and Malaysia. As the brand prepares to expand its footprint to additional overseas markets, Baldo emphasized that DTI remains an essential partner in helping them navigate complex international trade regulations, join major trade expositions, and build lasting B2B networks with fellow MSMEs. Local roots to global reach Inside the fair, the potential of the coconut continued to unfold across aisle after aisle of organic skincare, personal care products, and eco-friendly home essentials. Yet behind every innovative item on display is a unified government effort to elevate local enterprises. Through joint initiatives, agencies like the DTI and the PCA work hand-in-hand to equip MSMEs with technical guidance, market readiness, and the tools needed to scale for international export. Further, through SM for MSMEs, Filipino entrepreneurs gain opportunities to connect with customers, build networks, test their products in the market, and open new pathways for growth. That local traction is already fueling a global impact. Driven in part by this rising wave of commercialized innovations, Philippine coconut exports surged by 34.4 percent in 2025 to reach $3.6 billion, accounting for a vital share of the country's $84.48 billion total export revenues. With such momentum, the sector is positioned to shape not just the future of agriculture, but the trajectory of the national economy. The coconut remains a testament to Filipino resilience: a resource that sustains rural communities, powers international trade, and anchors a growing culture of innovation. In the Philippines, it seems, there is no limit to what the humble coconut and innovative Filipino minds can do.

‘They’re concrete acts of stewardship’: Cayetano defends Laguna Lakeshore project amid row with Lacson. Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano has again defended the Laguna Lakeshore project, highlighting the remarkable progress of the Laguna Lake within the jurisdiction of Taguig City in recent years and its vast untapped potential. Cayetano, in a recent Facebook livestream, also called for better stewardship of God’s creation, as he defended his city’s decision to pursue infrastructure projects within the Lakeshore. “Nung congressman pa ako ng 1998, naging passion ko na po kung paano pagandahin ang Laguna Lake. Nagkaroon lang po siyempre ako ng opportunity sa side ng Taguig dahil nga ito ang aking home city… Napakarami po kasing gamit ng lake (Back when I was a congressman in 1998, improving Laguna Lake became a passion of mine. Naturally, I had the opportunity to focus on the Taguig side since it is my home city... After all, the lake has so many uses),” Cayetano said in two August 27 live streams along the Taguig Lakeshore. “Ang pagiging sa gobyerno, ang pagiging public servant — hindi po kami ang may-ari ng resources… Kami po ay stewards, tagapamahala lang. Lahat ng tao kahit na wala sa gobyerno, meron po tayong obligasyon maging good stewards (Being in government, being a public servant—we do not own the resources... We are merely stewards, managers. Everyone, even those outside of government, has an obligation to be good stewards),” he said. Cayetano related the City of Taguig's lakeshore projects as concrete acts of stewardship, designed to protect the lake from erosion, pollution, and illegal settlements while ensuring public access for all. “Nung ginawa y’ung C6 or road dike, basically, pinoprotect po y’ung lakeshore. And part of its protection is not only na huwag mag-erode, (but para) hindi bahayan ng informal centers kasi kung mabahayan yung dumi, dito mapupunta sa lawa. The other thing is to make it for public use (When you built the C6 or road dike, basically, you were protecting the lakeshore. And part of its protection is not only to prevent erosion, (but to) not house informal centers because if they were houses, the waste would end up in the lake. The other thing is to make it for public use),” the senator explained. Cayetano also countered allegations of land-grabbing by pointing out that the local government actually reserved the area for public use, reversing the historical pattern of private encroachment along the lakeshore. “May allegations na may kinakamkam kami. Hindi ko lang alam kung pag sinabing kami, kung kaming mga Cayetano, kung ako, o kami ng ibang leaders… Doon sa bandang gitna, marami na pong private (land) kasi may 1,100 hectares ng lupa na nasa labas ng road dike. Meron po doon na private property, merong gobyerno (There are allegations that we are appropriating land for ourselves. I am just not sure who is meant by ‘we’—whether it refers to us Cayetanos, just me, or us together with other leaders... In the middle section, there is a lot of private land, as there are 1,100 hectares situated outside the road dike. There are both private properties and government-owned lands there),” he said. “Pero ito lahat po, precisely ni-reserve at ginawan ng paraan ng local government na maging public para hindi kamkamin. So baliktad sa allegation na kinakamkam. Titingnan niyo po y’ung history. Maraming kumakamkam po ng lupa dito. Pero ang history po ng Cayetano ay tumutulong na maging good stewards para sa gobyerno (But all of this was precisely reserved and secured by the local government for public use to prevent it from being seized by private interests. So, the allegation that it is being grabbed is the exact opposite of the truth. If you look at the history—there are many who do grab land here. But the Cayetanos’ track record shows they help act as good stewards for the government),” he emphasized. On Saturday, August 29, Sen. Panfilo “Ping” Lacson released further information and identified four parcels of illegally reclaimed land in Taguig which he said have been issued fraudulent land titles, while four others lack plotted title lots in the Land Registration Authority’s (LRA) digital file. Lacson said his public disclosure of the details of the initial findings is to dispel insinuations that his earlier exposes on illegal reclamation activities in Taguig City were “fake news.” “Since Senator Cayetano keeps publicly asking for evidence, I’ll give it to him, in the spirit of public interest,” he said. In response, Cayetano again, took to Facebook livestream to refute Lacson’s allegations, referring to the former national police chief as a “Marites” and a “Senator-Judge Troll.” “That senator-judge has been trolling me almost every day. It’s all just gossip, or, as they say, inconclusive, argumentative, and hearsay,” Cayetano said. “So, if Senator Lacson—our senator-judge-troll—wishes to inspect the developments at the lake, he is most welcome,” he stressed.

Dozens of soldiers killed or arrested after an apparent mutiny in Niger's capital, state TV reports. NIAMEY, Niger (AP) — Dozens of soldiers were killed or arrested after a group of young troops attempted a mutiny in Niger's capital in what was seen as a major threat to the country's ruling junta, according to a state television broadcast and analysts. It was the culmination of nearly 24 hours of unrest that appeared to be staged by young soldiers aggrieved over the worsening militant violence under the country's military junta. Russia's Africa Corps provided aerial and ground support to local forces to resist the rebellion, according to analysts and diplomats. State broadcaster RTN showed footage of dozens of mostly young soldiers being paraded in public after sustained gunfire and explosions were heard overnight into Saturday at a key military base located within Niamey's main airport and near the presidential palace. "The fighting lasted a few hours in several places, which allowed (security forces) to gradually control the situation, arrest and incapacitate these moody soldiers," state TV reported. The whereabouts of military leader Abdourahamane Tchiani were unclear. Senior Nigerien military officers visited the Africa Corps base at the airport "and expressed gratitude to its servicemen for their assistance in suppressing the rebellion," Russian media quoted Moscow's Ambassador to Niger Viktor Voropayev as saying. The rebelling soldiers had camped at the military base until late Saturday while the presidential guard secured the presidential palace and was deployed to regain control of the base, analysts and diplomats said. The loyalist forces have regained the "upper hand at least at the airport (and base)," according to Wassim Nasr, a senior research fellow at the Soufan Center. Some forces were, however, heading to the capital and it remained unclear if they were coming to support the mutiny or the junta, Nasr added. The Associated Press could not independently confirm whether the Nigerien security forces regained full control of the base. Unrest started with a hostage situation Some of the mutinous soldiers came from the southwest of the country, among the regions worst-hit by insecurity, diplomats and analysts said. The state broadcaster stopped its live transmission for some time on Saturday morning before it resumed. It broadcast a statement from Niger's Defense Minister Gen. Salifou Mody saying a group of soldiers took some officers hostage at the base and shot at "sensitive sites" in a "break with the discipline and military regulations." The airport is a strategic hub that hosts a Nigerien air force base as well as the headquarters of the joint Niger-Burkina Faso-Mali military force. All three neighbors are now under military rule, following a string of coups in Africa's Sahel region, but are struggling with insecurity. Niger's junta came to power after a 2023 coup which it said was prompted by the elected government's inability to stem armed violence. Since then, the impoverished West African country of more than 25 million people has severed ties with longtime Western security partners, turning instead to Russia. But the junta has been unable to stem militant violence and rampant killing of security forces, fueling unrest within the military, observers say. The ruling military council, known as the National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland, called for unity. "Our Defense and Security Forces are mobilized for the Defense of the Fatherland. Let us remain united, vigilant and supportive," it said in a Facebook post. Algeria's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement that the country has assured Niger, its southeastern neighbor, of its "full solidarity and firm support, with a view to overcoming this ordeal and promoting a rapid return to stability." Niger's military junta has struggled to stem violence, fueling unrest It is the third time this year that the base at the Diori Hamani International Airport has been attacked, after two earlier assaults by jihadi rebels. The attacks are "becoming commonplace and will continue to fuel unrest and aggravate tensions within the army ranks," said Heni Nsaibia, West Africa senior analyst at Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, a conflict monitor. "Deteriorating insecurity drove the coups that swept across the central Sahel, and the latest events show how these same pressures are now fueling unrest within the militaries that seized power," Nsaibia said. The mutiny adds to pressure on the military authorities, which have been unable to contain deadly jihadi violence. Before the 2023 coup, Niger had been the West's last reliable partner in the region in battling jihadists linked to al-Qaida and the Islamic State group in the Sahel. However, the country's security forces, aided by Russia's Africa Corps, have been overstretched on multiple fronts by jihadi groups whose repeated attacks in the last year have resulted in mass casualties within the military.

Influencer pleads guilty to criminal impersonation for viral pranks. PHOENIX (AP) — A social media influencer known for posting viral videos of pranks has pleaded guilty to criminal impersonation in Arizona for posing as an employee of businesses in a Phoenix suburb and orchestrating brief but chaotic takeover attempts. The outcome was welcomed by observers who said it could serve as a reminder to seekers of viral fame that stunts that cross the line legally can lead to serious ramifications. Heston James Cobb, who posts as “Heston James,” was arrested in July 2025 after police in Tempe say he and others went into businesses posing as workers, entered employee-only areas and refused to leave when asked to do so. He entered his plea Friday. In one video Cobb, wearing a Chipotle Mexican Grill shirt, told restaurant staff he was going to “clean house” before a group of men wearing dark shirts flooded into the eatery and ignored requests to leave. One man posing as an employee cleaned a tabletop with a mop. Investigators said the videos had millions of views and potentially generated large amounts of income. Vicki Lopez, an attorney representing Cobb, declined to comment Saturday. The Associated Press left a message with Cobb’s TikTok account seeking comment. Steve Chucri, president of the Arizona Restaurant Association, said he hopes Cobb’s punishment is “severe” to deter copycats. “There’s no place for it,” Chucri said. “That’s the last thing we need to put up with in the restaurant industry. The amount of money it takes to operate today is expensive.” Chucri said the association does not offer any formal training or advice to restaurants on dealing with social media pranksters, and he hopes it does not come to that. “We’re a society of civility,” Chucri said. “We shouldn’t have to.” Matthew Pittman, a social media professor at the University of Tennessee in Knoxville, hopes the arrest will be a warning to influencers about boundaries when creating prank or satirical content. Pittman said he and others who teach aspiring content creators generally stress that “real world norms and laws” extend into the digital world. “So doing something that is illegal in real life would also be illegal on social, even if you are doing it for content,” he said. “This is a clear case of going beyond what the law allows.” Among the recent cases he cited was an influencer in Long Island, New York, who was arrested last year after a series of pranks. They included videos of him going to eateries; pouring food such as raw eggs or beans over his head; and then running off, leaving the mess to be cleaned by others. “Every few years a YouTuber, influencer or prank content creator goes a little too far, gets in trouble, and reminds the rest of us creators that digital actions can have real world consequences,” Pittman said. Cara Hawkins-Jedlicka, a communications professor at Washington State University who teaches about content creation, said it’s not enough for influencers to stay within the law. They also need to have basic empathy. “When is it pulling a prank, and when it is being cruel?” Hawkins-Jedlicka said. “Before anything else, this is truly kind of unkind. This influencer was really only thinking about himself and how can I take advantage of this community.”

LPA inside PAR may develop into tropical depression ‘Pilandok’. A low-pressure area (LPA) that entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) on Saturday evening, Aug. 29, may develop into a tropical depression within the next few hours, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said Sunday, Aug. 30. PAGASA weather specialist Obet Badrina said the LPA was located 1,340 kilometers east of extreme Northern Luzon as of Sunday morning. “Base po sa pinakahuling datos natin, itong low-pressure area na ito ay posible po maging bagyo within the day at tatawagin po natin itong Bagyong ‘Pilandok’ (Based on our latest data, this low-pressure area may develop into a tropical cyclone within the day and will be called ‘Pilandok’),” Badrina said. The LPA could also affect the southwest monsoon or “habagat,” which continues to bring rains over parts of Luzon. “Inaasahan din natin na sa pagkilos nitong low-pressure area na ito, maging bagyo man po, posibleng palakasin ulit nito ang habagat (Meanwhile, as this low-pressure area moves, whether it develops into a tropical cyclone or not, it could possibly strengthen the southwest monsoon),” Badrina said. He said PAGASA would continue to monitor how the LPA could interact with the habagat. “Sa ngayon po kailangan pa rin natin ito imonitor kung paano yung magiging dynamics po o makakaapekto itong low-pressure area na maaaring maging bagyo sa habagat (For now, we still need to monitor its dynamics and how this low-pressure area, which may develop into a tropical cyclone, could affect the southwest monsoon),” Badrina said. The habagat remains the weather system mainly affecting Luzon as of Sunday. Rainy conditions are expected particularly over Ilocos Region, Cordillera Administrative Region, Central Luzon, Metro Manila, Calabarzon, and Occidental Mindoro. The rainfall outlook for Sunday showed that Ilocos Sur, Pangasinan, La Union, Benguet, Bataan, Zambales, Tarlac, and Pampanga could receive 100 to 200 millimeters or rain, considered heavy to intense. Metro Manila, Ilocos Norte, Abra, Apayao, Kalinga, Ifugao, Mountain Province, Nueva Vizcaya, Nueva Ecija, Bulacan, Rizal, Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, and Occidental Mindoro could receive 50 to 100 millimeters, or moderate to heavy rainfall. On Monday, Aug. 31, 100 to 200 millimeters of rain could affect Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, La Union, Pangasinan, Abra, Benguet, Zambales, and Bataan. Fifty to 100 millimeters could prevail over Apayao, Kalinga, Ifugao, Mountain Province, Tarlac, Pampanga, Bulacan, Metro Manila, Rizal, Cavite, Batangas, and Occidental Mindoro. By Tuesday, Sept. 1, 100 to 200 millimeters of rain could affect Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, Abra, Benguet, and Zambales. Batanes, Apayao, Kalinga, Ifugao, Mountain Province, La Union, Pangasinan, Tarlac, Bataan, and Pampanga could receive 50 to 100 millimeters of rainfall. Despite the possible strengthening of the habagat, Badrina said rainfall over the western section of Luzon could decrease by Monday or Tuesday. “Posibleng mabawasan yung mga pag-ulan na mararanasan po natin partikular na sa western section ng Luzon sa araw ng Lunes o araw ng Martes (Rainfall that will be experienced, particularly over the western section of Luzon, could possibly decrease on Monday or Tuesday),” Badrina said. However, he urged the public to remain cautious as flash floods and landslides remain possible, particularly in western Luzon. Meanwhile, PAGASA is also monitoring Tropical Depression Saudel, formerly called “Obet.” Saudel was located 1,105 kilometers west-northwest of extreme Northern Luzon and is not directly affecting the country. “Sa ngayon ay hindi naman ito direktang nakakaapekto sa ating bansa (For now, it is not directly affecting the country),” Badrina said. The rest of Luzon and the Visayas may experience cloudy skies, while Mindanao is expected to generally have fair weather, although localized rain showers and thunderstorms remain possible.

Russian strike on a Ukrainian warehouse kills 37 in the war's deadliest attack this year. MYLA, Ukraine (AP) — A Russian drone struck a warehouse west of Kyiv that Ukrainian officials say was storing shells, mines and other ammunition, sparking massive explosions and fires that swept through dozens of nearby homes and buildings and killing 37 people. The Friday night attack on the warehouse in Myla, a village in the Bucha district, was the war's deadliest attack this year and came on the second of three days of nearly round-the-clock Russian strikes that have severely disrupted life in and around the Ukrainian capital. Attacks on the capital and, to a lesser extent, the rest of Ukraine have been nearly constant since Thursday. Kyiv officials say Russia builds up missile stocks and launches major attacks every few days, hoping to exhaust Ukrainian defenses through the sheer weight of numbers. The warehouse strike sparked fires that raced through homes and damaged at least 50 residential buildings, said Tymur Tkachenko, who heads the local regional military administration. He was later cited by local media as saying 34 of the people killed were residents of a care home for elderly and disabled people. More than 370 people were evacuated. The blasts rocked Myla, causing people to frantically seek cover. "At about 8 p.m., the drone hit a warehouse somewhere and then the detonation began," Oleksandr Vodolaz, a village resident, told The Associated Press. "No one knew that weapons were stored there." Another local, Zhanna Kravchuk, said she had so many questions about what happened. "Why are weapons like this ... in warehouses and not on the front lines where they would help?" she said. As crews raced to get people to safety and extinguish blazes, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attack as a "terrible situation" and said it appeared to be the result of "terrible negligence on the part of those who stored explosives right next to people." He noted that Ukrainian law forbids the storage of ammunition close to people's homes and said criminal proceedings had been opened. "Those who allowed this to happen must be held accountable for their decisions," the president said. Kyiv investigates warehouse targeted in attack In a social media post Saturday, Zelenskyy shed more light on the situation. "The first strike was on an ammunition storage site that definitely shouldn't have been there – a Defense Forces storage facility. Shells, mines, other ammunition, and drones detonated." Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi didn't specify what was in the warehouse, but he referenced a July attack on the Kyiv suburb of Vyshneve that struck an ammunition depot, killing 22 people and triggering detonations and fires that tore through nearby homes. "Unfortunately, we can already see that the terrible tragedy in Vyshneve did not become a lesson," Koretskyi said. "In the fifth year of a full-scale invasion, making the same mistakes is criminal negligence. And all those guilty, without exception, must be severely punished so that such situations do not happen again." The 37 killed surpassed the 31 who died in a July 2 strike on Kyiv, which had been the war's deadliest attack of 2026. Russia's Defense Ministry said it hit a warehouse in Myla that was storing components and launch boosters for long-range drones. It also said it attacked the ports of Mykolaiv and Izmail, and a logistics center and warehouse facilities storing parts for Ukraine's Flamingo cruise missiles in the Kyiv region. Russian jet-powered drones pose a problem for Kyiv Russian strikes damaged homes and apartment blocks in the southern Kherson region on Saturday, killing two people and wounding 27 more, including a child, Oleksandr Prokudin, head of the region administration, said in a statement. Prokudin said earlier in the week that Russia had intensified its attacks on critical infrastructure in the region, which is about 70% under Russian control. He also urged tens of thousands of residents to move to safer regions because of the possibility of prolonged power and heating outages this winter. Although officials haven't said whether they were used in the warehouse attack, Russia has significantly increased its use of jet-powered drones, and their numbers will keep growing as Moscow sees their effectiveness, Pavlo Palisa, deputy head of Ukraine's presidential office, told reporters Friday. "Means of attack always outpace means of defense. We will certainly need to adapt. It will take time," Palisa said. He said interceptor drones currently available to Ukraine, which could theoretically intercept jet-powered drones, have not yet demonstrated the expected effectiveness, though Ukraine is working on solutions. Ukraine vows to increase long-range strikes Meanwhile, Ukraine has stepped up its long-range attacks on Russian military industries and energy facilities in recent months. The attacks, which use domestically made drones, are meant to cut into a source of Moscow's war funding and make Russians feel the consequences. In his evening statement to the nation Friday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv hoped to increase its long-range strikes to reach 1000 drone launches every day. "Right now, we average over 300 of our long-range sanctions," Zelenskyy said, his preferred term for Kyiv's long-range attacks that have also lately targeted Russian large-scale online retailers. "There must be more. We have a very specific goal, and we will achieve it." Moscow's forces destroyed 313 Ukrainian drones overnight, Russia's Defense Ministry said Saturday. Ukrainian drone attacks wounded 11 people in Russia's Rostov region, Gov. Yuri Slyusar said. Writing on social media, he said that nine people were hospitalized, including four children.

Trump's Greenland threats cast a shadow on Iceland's vote on whether to trigger EU membership talks. REYKJAVIK, Iceland (AP) — Voters in Iceland went to the polls Saturday to decide whether the country should resume long-stalled negotiations to become a member of the European Union, in the shadow of U.S. President Donald Trump's threats to control nearby Greenland. The yes-or-no referendum question is simple enough for the 265,000 or so eligible voters: Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union? A yes vote would trigger negotiations with the EU's executive branch, the European Commission, covering 35 areas, from the economy to human rights. Some supporters believe the European Union could offer protections if Trump ever made similar threats against Iceland. They also see economic stability in joining the bloc. If voters reject the proposal, that's it, for a generation at least. Opponents have rallied around the threat EU membership would pose to Iceland's rich fishing stocks and the fact that Iceland already reaps benefits from being in the EU's frictionless single market and the Schengen free-travel zone. Experts expect a close vote. More than 20% of voters cast early ballots in advance of election day, Iceland's national broadcaster RÚV said. "This has been a tight race, extremely exciting," said Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir, whose platform was based in part on rejoining the EU, after she voted. "It's lifted discussions about the EU, about Iceland's place in the world, about our general geopolitical situation and status to a higher level." Nearby Greenland casts a shadow over referendum When Trump talked about U.S. control of Greenland, particularly at the start of this year, he shifted the mood in Iceland, just 180 miles (290 km) from the self-governing territory of Denmark, a longtime U.S. ally. Iceland is a NATO member, but nonetheless some of its citizens were particularly alarmed when Trump mistakenly named their country four times while speaking about his designs on Greenland. Though Trump has indicated he won't use force to seize Greenland, his interest doesn't appear to have cooled. The underlying worry among many in Iceland is clear — if Greenland is seized, is Iceland next? The ensuing question is clear too: if yes, does EU membership provide a bulwark against any new Trump ambition in the North Atlantic? Iceland's left-leaning coalition government, elected in 2024, certainly thinks so, and that's largely why it moved forward with the EU referendum that it had planned for next year. After more than a decade, EU membership is back on the agenda EU talk is nothing new in Iceland, which formally ended its previous effort to join the bloc in 2015, largely over concerns about what membership would mean for its rich fish resources. The hefty cod and haddock catches from the chilled Arctic waters around Iceland are central to the national identity too. Descendants of Vikings who settled in Iceland have lived off the sea for centuries. With much of the country's economy geared toward its lucrative and well-managed fishing industry, fishing rights have been a talking point in the run-up to the referendum. Joining the 27-nation EU would require Iceland to be part of the bloc's common fisheries policy that would allow Spanish, Dutch and other trawlers into its waters. The government has indicated it would seek a special arrangement, potentially a full opt-out from the policy. If the vote is approved, it would not be the final say for Iceland. Voters would then have to either approve or reject the membership agreement it negotiates. Fish is not just an economic matter; it's part of the national identity For many, Iceland's national identity and ultimately its culture is on the ballot too. Iceland, which gained independence from Denmark in 1944, has a proud history of refusing to be pushed around by bigger and richer European nations. It even fought — and won — the so-called Cod Wars with Britain in the 1970s over its fishing grounds. Backers of EU membership say it's best for Iceland to get closer to its European neighbors to combat issues that don't respect borders, such as climate change. They also say the euro would bring more stability than Iceland's volatile króna currency and EU membership would lower inflation and interest rates. "Being in good connection and good relations with Europe is absolutely the best thing that Iceland has ever done and should continue," Haukur Hallsson said after voting in favor of EU discussions. "Iceland should definitely look more to Europe than the White House at this moment." Opponents say the current setup is just right and that Iceland already enjoys all the benefits of European integration without the sovereignty compromises that inevitably come with full membership. They say their vote in Europe's Parliament would be small and they prefer to cut some of their own trade deals, such as one with China. Agust Hallvardsson said he voted against the measure because the independence of Iceland's fisheries and agriculture is vital. "What's happening in the EU is not to my liking," Hallvardsson said. "It's like a big burning ship. I think they need to, you know, put their things right before we join them. And I think we're better off alone."

Hovland surges to 1-shot lead with cast of challengers lined up behind him. ATLANTA (AP) — Viktor Hovland finally got a little separation Saturday, Aug. 29, at the Tour Championship, and all he had to do was finish with six consecutive putts of 7 feet or longer for a 5-under 65. All that got him was a one-shot lead in a season finale very much up for grabs. Four of those putts were for birdie, two of them for par, all of them important going into a final round at East Lake where every shot can seem so important. Scoring has felt low. With some of the pins, it hasn't felt easy. Rory McIlroy and Ludvig Aberg each referenced similarities to Aronimink for the PGA Championship, where 28 players were separated by two shots midway through the third round. Only 29 players are at East Lake and everyone is under par. Hovland rolled in a pair of 8-foot birdie putts at the end to put him at 15-under 195, one shot ahead of Tour Championship newcomer Ryan Gerard, who played bogey-free for a 66. Scottie Scheffler (66) and Chris Gotterup (67), who have combined for five PGA Tour titles this year, were three shots behind at 12-under 198. They were joined by sentimental favorite, 46-year-old Adam Scott, and Aberg. Both shot 65 in search of their first win this year. Also in the mix was Rory McIlroy, who had two bogeys, settled for par on the par-5 closing hole and still shot 63 to get within five shots. He was joined by Cameron Young, whose double bogey on the 10th hole set him back in a round of 68. “It’s pretty bunched up around 11- and 12-under par there," Hovland said. “I mean, you’ve seen some 62s out there. You can take it low. So it was nice to get a little bit of distance, especially from the group of guys that are around that number. They’re capable of shooting nothing tomorrow. So that gives me a little bit of a cushion for tomorrow. I’m still going to have to bring a nice, solid round." At stake Sunday is $10 million to the winner, the largest official payoff in golf for a single tournament, and the FedEx Cup title that comes with a five-year exemption on the PGA Tour. Hovland won the FedEx Cup in 2023 when he steamrolled through a three-tournament postseason and won the last two. This might not feel the same if he were to win on Sunday, though the Norwegian would happily leave town with two trophies. Hovland was at his best on the greens coming down the stretch — 11 feet for birdie on the 13th, 18 feet to save par on the 14th, 11 feet for birdie on the peninsula-green 15th, a 7-foot par putt on the 16th and his closing birdies. Gerard scrambled beautifully, especially on the back nine, birdied both par 5s and stayed in the game for a chance at his first win this year, and possibly an easy decision to be a pick for the Presidents Cup. But it was a big test of patience waiting to a chance to attack. “Then when you do get that, try to take advantage and step on the gas there a little bit,” he said. That's what McIlroy did, starting out seven shots behind with little to lose. He figured he would need another round like 63 to even contemplate a fourth FedEx Cup title. He has been around for all the iterations of resetting points and starting strokes into the season finale. What he can't recall is a traffic jam at the top, or last place being at 3-under par. “It speaks to the standard of the golfers that are here,” McIlroy said. “But it also speaks to the slightly different test that we are getting after the redesign, as well.” Scheffler also played bogey-free and rued not taking advantage of a few more birdie chances in the 8- to 12-foot range. But he's right in the mix as he closes out a season of astonishing consistency that leaves him on the cusp of replacing Tiger Woods on the career money list. In the middle of the congestion was Scott, who has a chance to win for the first time since 2020. “It’s a good spot — within striking distance,” Scott said. “It’s so congested, though, it’s going to need a really great round. I think there’s someone lurking who’s going to have that.”

DSWD taps volunteers to keep relief food pack stocks replenished. The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) is turning to volunteers to help replenish its supply of family food packs following the distribution of millions of relief packs to disaster-affected communities in recent weeks. Volunteers are being welcomed at the Luzon Disaster Resource Center (LDRC) in Pasay City and the Visayas Disaster Resource Center (VDRC) in Mandaue City, Cebu, where repacking operations are conducted from Monday to Saturday. DSWD National Resource and Logistics Management Bureau (NRLMB) officer-in-charge Director Jun Eso said the production hubs are open to volunteers from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. DSWD has been replenishing its family food pack inventory after millions of packs were distributed to families affected by the southwest monsoon or “habagat” and tropical cyclones Luis, Maymay, and Neneng. Before the habagat-enhanced rains, the department had reached its five-million family food packs prepositioning target, with the packs distributed among about 1,000 warehouses nationwide. DSWD Secretary Rex Gatchalian earlier directed the NRLMB to accelerate production and replenish stocks to the five-million target as part of efforts to ensure that relief supplies are readily available when disasters strike. “Before po ng [bagyong] Luis, Maymay, at Neneng, we reached 5 million family food packs, and it’s a milestone for DSWD to have this strategically prepositioned all over the country. In case of any disaster, we could easily transport these family food packs to the affected communities (Before tropical cyclones Luis, Maymay, and Neneng, we reached five million family food packs, and it was a milestone for the DSWD to have these strategically prepositioned across the country. In case of any disaster, we could easily transport these family food packs to affected communities),” Eso said. Eso said volunteers can help the department meet its daily repacking targets as it works to restore its inventory. Interested individuals and groups are advised to coordinate with the NRLMB before visiting the facilities. Walk-ins are allowed, but the DSWD is encouraging volunteers to register in advance to help organize shifts. Volunteers must be at least 18 years old, while those below 18 must be accompanied by a guardian because heavy-duty machinery is used inside the warehouses. They are also advised to wear appropriate clothing, particularly closed shoes, for safety. “We would do brief orientation kung ano ’yung gagawin sa loob, and then at least 4 hours po [pwedeng] ma-render ng volunteer doon para ma-maximize din ’yung time natin while nandoon tayo kasi mayroon din tayong quota na niri-reach everyday (We would conduct a brief orientation on what volunteers will do inside, and volunteers may render at least four hours so we can maximize their time there because we also have a daily quota to meet),” Eso said.

Justin Arana activated for Gilas game vs Iran. Justin Arana has been activated for Gilas Pilipinas’ game against Iran in the fourth window of the 2027 FIBA World Cup Asian Qualifiers at the Mall of Asia Arena on Sunday, Aug. 30. The Converge big man is taking the spot of Carl Tamayo, who suffered an ankle injury in the Nationals’ 82-81 escape against Jordan in the first game of the window. It marks the first time Arana will be playing for the national team after also being called up before the start of the team’s preparation in the window. He will join Kai Sotto, June Mar Fajardo and AJ Edu at the frontlines with Justine Baltazar and Troy Rosario also patrolling the paint. Kevin Quiambao, Dwight Ramos and Chris Newsome are filling up the wings while Scottie Thompson, CJ Perez and Juan Gomez de Liaño will man the point guard spot. The Nationals will take on an Iranian team looking to bounce back from a tough 93-91 loss to New Zealand in the first game.

LPA develops into tropical depression ‘Pilandok’. The low-pressure area (LPA) inside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) has developed into a tropical depression and was locally named “Pilandok,” the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said on Sunday, Aug. 30. As of 10 a.m., the center of Tropical Depression Pilandok was estimated at 1,210 kilometers east of extreme Northern Luzon. It was moving west-northwestward at 15 kilometers per hour (kph), with maximum sustained winds of 45 kph near the center and gustiness of up to 55 kph. Pilandok is expected to continue moving west-northwestward through Monday, Aug. 31, before turning northwestward to north-northwestward for the remainder of the forecast period. PAGASA said the tropical depression is less likely to make landfall over the country and is expected to remain far from the Philippine landmass. The weather disturbance is also expected to be short-lived and remain a tropical depression throughout the forecast period before weakening into a remnant low over the Philippine Sea south of the southern islands of Japan on Tuesday, Sept. 1. PAGASA weather specialist Obet Badrina earlier said the agency would continue to monitor how Pilandok interacts with the southwest monsoon or “habagat.” For now, the habagat remains the weather system mainly affecting Luzon. The rainfall outlook for Sunday showed that Ilocos Sur, Pangasinan, La Union, Benguet, Bataan, Zambales, Tarlac, and Pampanga could receive 100 to 200 millimeters of rain, considered heavy to intense. Metro Manila, Ilocos Norte, Abra, Apayao, Kalinga, Ifugao, Mountain Province, Nueva Vizcaya, Nueva Ecija, Bulacan, Rizal, Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, and Occidental Mindoro could receive 50 to 100 millimeters of rain, considered moderate to heavy. On Monday, Aug. 31, 100 to 200 millimeters of rain could affect Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, La Union, Pangasinan, Abra, Benguet, Zambales, and Bataan. Fifty to 100 millimeters of rain could prevail over Apayao, Kalinga, Ifugao, Mountain Province, Tarlac, Pampanga, Bulacan, Metro Manila, Rizal, Cavite, Batangas, and Occidental Mindoro. By Tuesday, Sept. 1, 100 to 200 millimeters of rain could affect Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, Abra, Benguet, and Zambales. Batanes, Apayao, Kalinga, Ifugao, Mountain Province, La Union, Pangasinan, Tarlac, Bataan, and Pampanga could receive 50 to 100 millimeters of rainfall. Despite the possibility that Pilandok could strengthen the habagat, Badrina earlier said rainfall over the western section of Luzon could decrease by Monday or Tuesday. The public was nevertheless urged to remain alert for possible flash floods and landslides, particularly in areas that could receive prolonged or heavy rainfall.
