Weljon Mindoro suffers first career defeat vs Ocampo. Weljon Mindoro suffered a knockout defeat against Mexican veteran Carlos Ocampo in their 10-round non-title catchweight bout at the Galen Center in Los Angeles on Sunday, Aug. 30 (PH time). The Filipino pug just couldn’t sustain the impressive start to the bout and suffered a ninth round technical knockout defeat. The veteran Ocampo unloaded a slick right counter which landed to the jaw of Mindoro, who immediately went down after the hit. The 29-year-old Filipino managed to get back up and beat the count but his corner waved the flag, formally ending the fight at the 1:29 mark of the penultimate round. Undefeated prior to the contest, Mindoro was actually dictating the tempo in the early round, even opening a cut above Ocampo’s right eye with a big right hand in the third Ocampo, who has been in several title fights against Tim Tszyu and Sebastian Fundora, rallied back into the contest and began landing big hits during the middle rounds before finally drilling the decisive right hand in the ninth round. The World Boxing Council Federación Centroamericana de Boxeo middleweight crown was supposed to be at stake in the bout but Ocampo came in overweight at 165-pounds. Mindoro dropped to a 17-1-1 record with 16 knockouts while Ocampo improved to a 39-4 slate.

Cone amazed by Quiambao’s rapid improvement. Gilas Pilipinas head coach Tim Cone raved at the quick development of young forward Kevin Quiambao, who is now emerging as one of the team’s reliable players in the 2027 FIBA World Cup Asian Qualifiers. Quiambao, who has been playing superb for Gilas through the last two windows, stepped up big in the Nationals’ much-needed 82-81 win over Jordan at the Mall of Asia Arena on Friday, Aug. 28. The 6-foot-6 forward nailed a booming triple with 11.7 seconds left to break a 79-all deadlock and put Gilas ahead for good. He finished with 14 points and five rebounds after getting extended minutes on the floor due to the absence of Justin Brownlee and later on the injury to Carl Tamayo. “He came in as the young guys of the team when we put this together two and a half years ago. We said at that point that at some point, he's going to be the guy that takes over the program. Him and Carl,” said Cone. The veteran coach, however, admitted that he did not expect Quiambao to take such a big role at this point of his career but he nonetheless welcomes the fast growth of his prized forward. “They were the two young guns that were gonna come up and be our main guys at some point. I was expecting that to happen when they're 26, 27, 28 but it’s happening now when they are 23, 24 years old,” he added. Quiambao had a breakout performance in the July window when he fired 23 points in the tough 106-102 double-overtime defeat at the hands of New Zealand. His performance took off from there. “They got a tremendous future in front of them. I really enjoy coaching KQ. He's such a good kid too. Carl also. It’s really fun to coach those guys,” said Cone.

PH marks 75th anniversary of Mutual Defense Treaty with US. The Department of National Defense (DND) and the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Sunday, Aug. 30, marked the 75th anniversary of the Mutual Defense Treaty (MDT), an agreement which provides the legal and strategic framework for defense cooperation with the United States, giving both countries a basis for working together when faced with a common security threat. DND spokesperson Asst. Sec. Arsenio Andolong said the MDT remains a key part of Manila and Washington’s commitment to peace, stability, and the defense of a free and open Indo-Pacific. “As we commemorate the 75th anniversary of the Philippines-United States Mutual Defense Treaty, we honor an alliance that has endured through generations and has evolved to meet the demands of an increasingly complex security environment,” he said in a statement. The treaty was signed in Washington, D.C., on Aug. 30, 1951, recognizing that an attack in the Pacific on either country would endanger the peace of both, and obliges them to act together to meet the common danger. Over the past seven decades, the DND said the defense pact has served as a framework for sustained defense and security cooperation between Manila and Washington. The partnership has expanded from the original defense arrangement to exercises, maritime security cooperation, humanitarian assistance and disaster response, capability development, and greater interoperability between Filipino and American forces. “For seven decades, the MDT has provided a framework for sustained cooperation between the two countries, strengthening interoperability, enhancing defense capabilities, and contributing to peace, stability, and security in the Indo-Pacific region,” AFP public affairs office chief Col. Xerxes Trinidad said. The DND said the cooperation was significant because the Philippines faces security challenges in a region where maritime disputes and other threats require stronger defense capabilities and closer coordination with allies and partners. The DND also cited the growing scope and sophistication of bilateral and multilateral exercises and engagements as evidence of the alliance's continuing development. “The strength of our alliance is evident in the success, sophistication, and growing scope of our bilateral and multilateral exercises, engagements, and people-to-people exchanges,” Andolong noted. He said such efforts have enhanced interoperability and strengthened deterrence while demonstrating the two countries’ resolve to support regional security and stability. “As we look to the future, we remain committed to building a more sustainable, agile, and productive partnership anchored on mutual respect, shared interests, and adherence to international law,” Andolong concluded.

Kai’s knowledge, instincts ‘like a point guard’. Gilas Pilipinas head coach Tim Cone has nothing but praises for Kai Sotto in his first game back since fully recovering from an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury that sidelined him from national team duty for almost two years. The veteran mentor pointed out that more than Sotto’s length, the 7-foot-3 center has the basketball instinct and knowledge comparable to point guards, making the rest of his teammates better while he’s on the floor. “The thing about Kai, yes, he’s 7-foot-3 but his knowledge of the game, instinct for the game is like a point guard. He is like RJ Abarrientos or Juan Gomez de Liano,” said Cone after Gilas’ 82-81 win over Jordan. “He’s really that smart and that intelligent, that makes people around him better. Everybody’s better when he’s on the floor whether through passing, scoring or rolling, the attention he grabs, he just makes everybody better,” he added. And Cone certainly has the numbers to support that. Without Sotto, Gilas has not beaten teams inside the top 60 of the world rankings through the FIBA Asia Cup qualifiers and main tournament and the World Cup Asian qualifiers. When Sotto’s playing, Gilas is defeating teams way above its ranking in the likes of Latvia and New Zealand. And this time, against a potent Jordan team. Of course, Sotto’s length also made a ton of differences — evident in the final play when he swatted away what could have been Jordan’s game-winning attempt. “What was really big tonight was his defense patrolling against Al Dwairi who was a really top class center and also patrolling the paint especially in the second half not allowing Harris and Ybrahim to get to the rim on us,” Cone pointed out “And Olajuwon at the end. Remember, Olajuwon earlier was getting to the rim with impunity but the last play he get to the rim but of course Kai rejected him,” he added.

Binangonan e-library receives book donations. The Binangonan Municipal e-Library and Museum received a donation of grade school and junior high school textbooks from a private school in the municipality, expanding access to learning materials for local students and residents. The donation drive, spearheaded by both the Calumpang and Batingan campuses of the Child Jesus of Prague School (CJPS), aims to expand learning materials available to the public and foster an enriched academic environment for the youth across the municipality. Representatives from the Binangonan Municipal e-Library and Museum expressed their profound gratitude to the school administration, faculty, and students for their generosity. Vice Mayor Russel Ynares, whose initiative led to the establishment of the municipal library and museum, said that the turnover of books represents more than a charity drive; it serves as a cornerstone for building long-term institutional partnerships between the local government and the private educational institution. "This CJPS and municipal government initiative is just the beginning of a stronger collaboration between our local educational institutions and the municipal government. By working together, we can continuously elevate the quality of education and provide better learning opportunities for all Binangonan students," Ynares said. The newly donated textbooks will be integrated into the library’s growing collection, ensuring that public school students, researchers, and young learners have ready access to high-quality reference materials for the current school year. Officials from both CJPS and the local government led by the full support of Mayor Rhea Ynares, are optimistic that this collaborative framework will inspire other private and public organizations to invest in community-based learning initiatives, driving sustainable educational development across the province. The municipal library, in turn, is donating books and other learning materials to public schools in the municipality as part of its community literacy and e-learning programs for the people of the municipality.

10 days’ worth of rain falls on Manila in one day — DRRM office. Rainfall that lashed Manila on Saturday, Aug. 29, was equivalent to around 10 days’ worth of rain, triggering flooding in several parts of the city and sending more than 1,000 residents to evacuation centers, the Manila City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Department (MCDRRMD) said. Christian John Evangelista, MCDRRMD resident meteorologist and chief of research and planning, said the city recorded its highest daily rainfall at Dr. Alejandro Albert Elementary School in Sampaloc, reaching147.4 millimeters (mm). “Katumbas po ng sampung araw na ulan ang bumuhos sa Maynila kahapon (The rainfall that poured over Manila yesterday was equivalent to 10 days’ worth of rain),” Evangelista said. “Ang pinakamataas na narecord natin ay sa Dr. Albert ES na umaabot sa 147.4mm at ang pinakamataas na hourly rate ay bandang 4 p.m., 23.6mm (The highest rainfall we recorded was at Dr. Albert Elementary School, reaching 147.4 mm, while the highest hourly rate was recorded at around 4 p.m., at 23.6 mm).” Rainfall intensified at several points throughout the day, with the city experiencing two episodes of heavy to intense rain around 1 p.m. and 4 p.m. “Makikita po na tayo nakaranas ng dalawang episodes ng heavy to intense rainfall sa siyudad bandang 1 p.m. at 4 p.m. ( We experienced two episodes of heavy to intense rainfall in the city, around 1 p.m. and 4 p.m.) ,” Evangelista said. The rain intensified again around 1 p.m., when all four MCDRRMD monitoring stations reached the “Intense” category. After briefly easing, rainfall peaked again at around 4 p.m., with hourly readings ranging from 23.6 mm to 27.2 mm . Other monitoring stations also recorded significant rainfall, withCayetano Arellano High School at 143 mm, BASECO Evacuation Center at 135.8 mm, and Manila City Hall at 129.6 mm. The heavy downpour left several major roads flooded throughout the afternoon. MCDRRMD reported gutter-deep flooding along most of Taft Avenue and portions of España Boulevard. The Pedro Gil portion of Roxas Boulevard and the Magsaysay-V. Mapa area in Sta. Mesa recorded around eight inches of flooding, while Kalaw Avenue going toward Taft reached 10 inches, the deepest recorded in the city. “Sapat po ang dami ng ulan na ito upang makapagtala ng mga pagbaha lalo na po sa ating low-lying areas ( The amount of rainfall was enough to cause flooding, particularly in our low-lying areas) ,” Evangelista said. The afternoon rainfall also coincided with a sharp increase in evacuees. Data from the Manila Department of Social Welfare (MDSW) showed that the number of families and individuals staying in evacuation centers more than doubled between 2 p.m. and 4 p.m. on Saturday. As of 8 a.m. Sunday, Aug. 30 , a total of 367 families or 1,141 individuals were staying in evacuation centers across Manila. The biggest increases were recorded in Districts V and VI and BASECO . Don Bosco School in District VI sheltered 157 families, or 518 individuals, while the BASECO Evacuation Center sheltered 150 families, or 450 individuals . Manila City Social Welfare Officer Jay Dela Fuente said the MDSW provided evacuees with hot meals, dinner, sleeping mats, and breakfast . Meanwhile, the Market Administration Office (MAO) distributed doxycycline to vendors at the Central Market as part of the city’s efforts to help prevent leptospirosis amid the threat of flooding. Vendors were also reminded to take precautions and follow health protocols to protect themselves from illnesses associated with flood exposure. The MCDRRMD said the rainfall data showed how quickly heavy rain can translate into flooding, particularly in Manila’s low-lying areas.

Manila continues aid for over 1,000 evacuees as rains persist. The Manila city government continued providing food and other assistance to over 1,000 evacuees staying in evacuation centers on Sunday, August 30, as heavy rains brought by the southwest monsoon or habagat persisted in the capital. The Manila Department of Social Welfare (MDSW)distributed hot meals to evacuees to ensure their food needs were met while they temporarily remained in evacuation centers. MDSW personnel also continued monitoring the condition of families who evacuated from flood-affected areas and assessing their immediate needs. MDSW DirectorJay Dela Fuente visited evacuees at an evacuation center in Barangay 598, Damka Street, Sta. Mesa, Manila, to check on their condition and the assistance being provided. The continued response came as Metro Manila remained under an Orange Rainfall Warning on Sunday due to the southwest monsoon. The Manila city government also activated Code White , placing emergency and medical response teams on heightened readiness amid the inclement weather. The city's localized heavy rainfall advisory was issued at 10:45 a.m. Sunday warned that Manila could experience heavy to intense rainfall that may last for two to three hours . Residents were urged to remain alert for possible flash floods, avoid flooded and low-lying areas, and evacuate when necessary. The MDSW said it would continue attending to the needs of evacuees and providing immediate assistance while they remain in temporary shelters. Residents were also advised to monitor weather updates from the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA).

1,141 Manileños remain in evacuation centers amid habagat. A total of 367 families or 1,141 individuals are currently staying in active evacuation centers across Manila as the city continues to monitor communities affected by the Southwest Monsoon or Habagat, the Manila Department of Social Welfare (MDSW) reported Sunday, August 30. The latest evacuation center status, as of 8 a.m. on Aug. 30, showed that evacuees are being housed in facilities across the city, including areas in Districts 3, 5, and 6, as well as Baseco. The largest number of evacuees was recorded in District 6, where 171 families or 562 individuals were staying at various evacuation centers. This included 157 families or 518 individuals from Barangays 602 and 601 who were staying at Don Bosco School. Meanwhile, 150 families or 450 individuals from Blocks 1 Gasangan and 1 Aplaya were staying at the Baseco Evacuation Center. Other active evacuation centers included the Barangay 326 Hall, with eight families or 23 individuals; Barangay 333 Hall, with three families or nine individuals; DWO V (Sagat, Bahay Kalinga), with 35 families or 97 individuals; Barangay 598, with seven families or 28 individuals; Barangay 607 Covered Court, with three families or seven individuals; Barangay 893 Barangay Hall, with four families or eight individuals; and Barangay 894 Multipurpose Hall, with one individual. The MDSW said it has been assisting evacuees with hot meals, dinner, sleeping mats, and breakfast. The city government continues to monitor the situation in affected communities and evacuation centers amid the effects of the Habagat.

1,415 remain in Parañaque evacuation centers as habagat continues. A total of 1,415 residents remained in evacuation centers in Parañaque City Sunday morning as persistent rains brought by the southwest monsoon, or habagat, continued to threaten flood-prone communities. The City Social Welfare and Development Department said the figure was recorded at 7 a.m. Sunday, August 30, lower than the 1,906 evacuees recorded Saturday night, August 29, as heavy rains prompted residents in vulnerable areas to seek safer shelter. Mayor Edwin Olivarez ordered city officials and barangay authorities to keep evacuation centers operational and remain on alert for possible flooding and additional rainfall. The city government said 14 evacuation centers had been opened to accommodate residents affected by the weather disturbance, with seven facilities actively housing evacuees as of the latest count. Evacuation centers were opened in several barangays, including BF Homes, San Antonio, San Dionisio, and San Isidro, as local authorities continued to monitor conditions in low-lying and flood-prone areas. Olivarez also urged residents to remain vigilant and follow instructions from barangay officials and disaster response teams, particularly those living in areas vulnerable to rising floodwaters.

Heavy rains cause landslide in Taguig. Heavy rains caused a landslide and collapse of a wall of a house in Barangay Pembo, Taguig, on Aug. 29. The Pembo Fire & Rescue Brigade reported that the landslide occurred on Dahlia Street in the barangay. The team received a radio report of the incident at about 2:16 p.m. and went to the area. A family of 11 members was evacuated because of the incident. The Taguig City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office and City Social Welfare and Development Office arrived and conducted a preliminary hazard and welfare assessment. The affected area was cordoned off. They were followed by the City Search and Rescue, which conducted a structural and safety evaluation. The owner of the adjacent property where a construction was being conducted agreed to assist the affected family. Meanwhile, the Taguig City government cleared fallen trees in different barangays, including Central Signal and Western Bicutan. At 11:05 a.m. on Aug. 30, Metro Manila was under red rainfall warning.

The High Speed Hitters raise the curtain when they take on Thai guest team EST Cola at 1:30 p.m., while fancied Creamline and Nxled square off at 4 p.m. Vietnamese squad Ho Chi Minh and Farm Fresh clash in the 6:30 p.m. nightcap. Simple math: Adiong says VP Duterte allegedly spent P473,000 an hour in confidential funds. House prosecution panel "layman" spokesperson Lanao del Sur 1st district Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong used simple math to illustrate the scale of Vice President Sara Duterte's alleged misuse of the Office of the Vice President's (OVP) confidential funds. Adiong was referring to the P125 million in confidential funds that were spent by the OVP in just 11 days in December 2022. "Nung natapos na nilang gastusin in 11 days, by the way, kung i-quantify natin yung 11 days, P473,000 every hour ang nagagastos, para ma-consume, in 11 days, ang P125 million, ganun kabilis at kalaki yung paggasto ng P125 million in 11 days," Adiong said in an online interview. (But when they finished spending it in 11 days, by the way, if we quantify those 11 days, they were spending P473,000 every hour to consume the P125 million in 11 days. That is how fast and how large the spending of P125 million was in 11 days.) "Not mentioning the fact na in 11 days na yan, merong mga holidays diyan,” he noted, adding a punchline to the already absurd average. (Not mentioning the fact that there were holidays during those 11 days.) The OVP received the P125-million cash advance in December 2022 and reported utilizing the entire amount from Dec. 21 to Dec. 31, a period that state auditor Roderick Wamil earlier flagged during his testimony because the allocation was intended for the fourth quarter. The prosecution has also questioned an OVP explanation referring to obligations that had already been incurred before the money was released, arguing that this sits uneasily with the treatment of confidential funds as cash advances governed by specific rules on utilization. “Ang confidential funds nga is, ano 'yan cash advance 'yan. Why would you reimburse something that have already been implemented from the confidential funds, which is actually is intended for specific purpose, guided by a specific criteria on how you handle that, bawal 'yun,” Adiong said. (Confidential funds are cash advances. Why would you reimburse something that had already been implemented using confidential funds, which are actually intended for a specific purpose and guided by specific criteria on how they should be handled? That is prohibited.) Beyond the speed of the spending, prosecutors have questioned whether the geographic reach reflected in the records could realistically have been accomplished within the same compressed period. “Meron pang pag-distribute nung confidential funds in 11 days, 134 areas all over the country in one day, so paano mo mate-testify 'yun?” asked the assistant majority leader from Mindanao. (There was also the distribution of the confidential funds in 11 days, covering 134 areas all over the country in one day, so how can you testify to that?) The 11-day expenditure has become one of the central factual issues under article I of the articles of impeachment as the prosecution traces how the first P125-million confidential-fund tranche was requested, withdrawn, distributed and eventually liquidated. Adiong says the prosecution is placing particular weight on contemporaneous official records because they provide fixed reference points against which subsequent explanations from OVP officials can be measured. “Whatever testimony that they would give to the court, whatever narrative that they would provide to the court, still we go back to the documents, the official documents, at hindi nagsisinungaling yung official documents, at hindi nagsisinungaling yung figures na nagre-reflect doon sa official documents, as compared to Colonel Lachica, wala siyang pinirmahan,” Adiong said. (Whatever testimony that they would give to the court, whatever narrative they provide to the court, we still go back to the official documents. Official documents do not lie, and neither do the figures reflected in those official documents, unlike Colonel Lachica, who did not sign anything.) Can VP Sara be trusted with public funds? The prosecution’s concerns also extend to the rules governing who may handle and account for confidential funds, with Adiong arguing that an alleged breach of basic safeguards could have implications beyond accounting procedures. “Can we trust the Vice President with the resources of the government, knowing that the policy, a very basic policy, hindi pa niya masunod given the fact na she is a lawyer and she has been using confidential funds for over three years now?" Adiong said of the impeachment trial respondent. (Can we trust the Vice President with the resources of the government, knowing that she cannot even follow a very basic policy, given that she is a lawyer and has been using confidential funds for over three years now?) Joint Circular (JC) No. 2015-01 requires the head of an agency to oversee the use of confidential funds, maintain effective internal controls, approve cash advances and liquidation reports, and ensure compliance with the rules. The designated special disbursing officer (SDO), meanwhile, is responsible for actually disbursing and accounting for the funds. Adiong argued that Duterte’s previous experience with confidential funds as Davao City mayor makes the alleged departure from those rules at the OVP particularly relevant in assessing accountability. “Pero the mere fact na maski 'yung simpleng joint circular na alam mo namang may joint circular, kasi naging mayor ka, at saka gumagamit ka na ng confidential funds before ka pa naging Bise Presidente, tapos viniolate mo ito very simple lang na policy, hindi mo finallow, tapos nag-utos ka pa ng tao para i-disregard ito at i-violate ito,” Adiong said. (But the mere fact that you did not follow even this simple joint circular, which you knew existed because you had been a mayor and had already been using confidential funds before becoming Vice President, and then you violated this very simple policy and even instructed someone to disregard and violate it.) Former OVP SDO Gina Acosta testified that Duterte instructed her to turn over the confidential-fund cash to Lachica despite Acosta being the designated bonded officer accountable for the funds--an arrangement prosecutors contend violated the governing circular. For Adiong, that alleged departure from a basic safeguard raises a leadership question extending beyond the mechanics of accounting because the impeachment charge asks whether or not Duterte betrayed the public trust attached to her office. Adiong said the prosecution therefore intends to have the senator-judges assess the confidential-fund transactions against the standard of responsibility expected from an official entrusted with public money and constitutional power. “So that alone proves na meron talagang culpable violation of the Constitution, because ang sinabi naman sa Constitution, public office is a public trust. So how can you be trusted with the mandate you have given by the people, kung yung simpleng polisiya ng paggamit ng confidential funds ay binaliwala mo?” he noted. (So that alone proves that there really was a culpable violation of the Constitution, because the Constitution says public office is a public trust. So how can you be trusted with the mandate given to you by the people if you disregarded the simple policy governing the use of confidential funds?)

Parañaque offers free doxycycline to residents exposed to floodwaters. Mayor Edwin Olivarez has directed health centers in all 16 barangays of Parañaque City to remain open on Sunday, August 30, to provide doxycycline prophylaxis to residents who waded through or walked in floodwaters amid continued rains brought by the southwest monsoon, or habagat. The city government said residents exposed to floodwaters may proceed to the nearest health center for proper assessment and guidance from health personnel on the appropriate use of doxycycline. The preventive measure is intended to help reduce the risk of leptospirosis, a bacterial infection that may be contracted through exposure to water or soil contaminated with the urine of infected animals. Olivarez urged residents to prioritize their safety and avoid walking or wading through floodwaters whenever possible, particularly when they have cuts or open wounds. Residents who have been exposed to floodwaters and later develop symptoms such as fever, headache, muscle pain, or weakness were advised to seek immediate medical attention. The city government continues to monitor the situation and provide health services to residents affected by the rains.

Marikina conducts recovery ops amid bad weather. Despite the continuing inclement weather, the Marikina City government on Sunday, Aug. 30, began clearing and recovery operations in flood-affected areas following heavy rainfall brought by the southwest monsoon (Habagat). It said that skid loaders, heavy equipment, and clearing personnel were deployed in Barangays Malanday, Tumana, Nangka, and Sto. Niño to quickly remove garbage, mud, and debris. It added that cleanup operations will continue until the affected areas are fully cleared and cleaned up. Marikina City Mayor Maan Teodoro said doctors are also making rounds at evacuation camps to provide doxycycline as protection against leptospirosis, particularly for residents who waded through floodwaters. “Nagpabili na rin ako ng additional supplies pa para hindi tayo kulangin (I also ordered additional supplies so we won’t run short),” she added. Teodoro, together with her husband, Rep. Marcy Teodoro, and rescue teams, personally monitored the weather conditions since Saturday, Aug. 29, to closely oversee the situation in the city and ensure the safety of residents. Heavy rainfall on Saturday reportedly reached an average accumulated total of 136.6 millimeters from 6 a.m. to 7 p.m. By 10:29 p.m., the Marikina River had reached the third alarm level after its water level rose to 18 meters, prompting the city government to implement forced evacuations, particularly in low-lying areas. The third alarm level remained in effect until 3:30 a.m. on Sunday, with the river reaching a peak water level of 18.5 meters before gradually declining. As of 1 p.m., the Marikina River had returned to normal, with its water level at 14.9 meters.

Garcia, Nazario rule WR Bughouse Chess Open. International Master Jan Emmanuel Garcia and National Master Marc Christian Nazario overcame a slow start with a blistering finish in ruling the WR Bughouse Chess Open at the MICE Center in Quezon City over the weekend. Getting only one-day of practice, Garcia and Nazario, who named their team Bubu Chacha, still came out victorious after edging College of St. Benilde Blazers’ John Laurence Donguines and Daniel Baylosis, 2-1, in their best-of-three title duel to pocket the top purse worth P100,000. Losing the first match, Garcia, who is part of the team playing in next month’s World Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, and Nazario, who finished in the quarterfinals of the inaugural WR Bughouse Championship last month in Taguig, came roaring back by seizing the next two matches including the rubber. Metaboys’ Samson Lim III and Jerich Cajeras, who topped the qualification round, swept DCSK’s Noel dela Cruz and Timothy John So Kua in two outings to finish third place in this one-day meet backed by WR Chess’ Wadim Rosenstein, the Philippine Sports Commission, Quezon City and the NCFP. More than a hundred participants saw action and battled through eight grueling rounds for the eight seats to the playoff stage. Apart from the four semifinalists, Chronosphere’s IM Pau Bersamina and Rafiel Irvin Lacorte, Datamatics Red’s Mark Kevin Labog and John Michael Magpily, Ruy Lopez Kidz’s Zach Evan Orzame and Marco Piolo Sanido, and Stopper’s IM Michael Concio, Jr. and FIDE Master Alekhine Nouri also made the playoff cut.

300 Caraga cops train for BARMM parliamentary polls. CAMP RAFAEL C. RODRIGUEZ, Butuan City – Three hundred policemen of Police Regional Office 13 (PRO 13) have started to undergo a two-day training to serve as members of the PNP Special Electoral Board (SEB) for the 2026 Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) Parliamentary Election. The two-day training, which started on Saturday, Aug. 29, was conducted at the PRO13 Multi-Purpose Center here, as part of the preparations to ensure the effective, orderly, and credible conduct of the upcoming parliamentary election. The training, conducted by the Commission on Elections (Comelec), focused on equipping PNP personnel with the knowledge and practical skills necessary to effectively perform their duties as SEB members. Topics included the General Instructions for the Electoral Board, particularly the procedures for voting, counting, and transmission of election results. Participants were also provided with a guide to the Automated Counting Machine Kit, including its proper operation through hands-on exercises. Regional Public Information Office (RPIO) chief of PRO 13 Police Lt. Col. Jennifer S. Ometer also said the training covered contingency procedures for addressing technical concerns that may arise during the election. “Kasali sa training ay yun iba pang mga dapat gawin in relation sa BARMM Parliamentary Election,” RPIO chief of PRO 13 added. Keynote speakers during the training – PRO 13 Director Police Brig. Gen. Rolindo M Suguilon and Caraga Region Comelec Regional Director Attorney Edwin O. Cadungog. “Let us demonstrate the highest level of discipline and professionalism as we fulfill our mandate in support of the Commission on Elections and our fellow Filipinos during the 2026 BARMM Parliamentary Election,” said Brig. Gen. Suguilon, in his opening remarks.

106 barangays in Cordillera warned of landslides due to continuous rains. BAGUIO CITY -- The Mines and Geosciences Bureau (MGB) Cordillera warned 106 barangays located in landslide-prone areas that they could be potentially affected by landslides due to the incessant rains experienced by the southwest monsoon or "habagat". The agency said that Benguet province has 24 landslide-prone areas in the towns of Atok, Bokod, Itogon, La Trinidad, and Tublay, including Baguio City, while Kalinga has the largest concentration with 50 areas in Tabuk City, Pinukpuk, and Rizal, particularly barangay Liwan. In Ifugao, there are 22 high-risk areas in the towns of Aguinaldo and Alfonso Lista, while in the town of Paracelis, there are seven barangays in Mountain Province and three barangays in Conner, Apayao. The MGB said that the two barangays are both located in mountainous areas, and with the continuous rains experienced by the region for a month and with the continued rains in September, the risk of sudden landslides is high. In PAGASA's August 30, 2-26 Weather Advisory No.30, the province of Benguet, including Baguio City, Ilocos Sur, La Union, Pangasinan, Bataan, Zambales, Tarlac, and Pampanga, will experience Orange Rainfall from 100-200 mm, while some parts of the Cordillera will experience 5-100 mm rainfall. The MGB-Cordillera called on provincial, city, and municipal governments and councils to strictly monitor landslide-prone areas and conduct forced evacuation of residents living in mountainous areas threatened by landslides.

Norway's new king pays tribute to his late father as tens of thousands mourn. OSLO, Norway (AP) — King Haakon VIII of Norway used his first speech in his new role to eulogize his father, King Harald V, as a loving parent and dedicated monarch a day after he died at 89. “We are in mourning. At the same time, it brings us comfort and strength to know that so many are mourning with us,” the king said wearing a black suit as his speech was shown live on public television. After Harald V’s death on Friday morning, the crown prince became King Haakon VIII immediately. He thanked the people for their outpouring of compassion and remembered what a loving father and husband Harald had been. Tens of thousands of mourners paid their respects, placing flowers and condolence cards outside the royal palace in Oslo, where the coffin arrived late Friday from the hospital. Across the country, churches and city halls opened specially so people could light candles, and write their thoughts about the deceased king in condolence books. “It has been a powerful and moving experience to see the Palace Square filled with people, flowers, messages of condolence, and candles. Thank you so much,” 53-year-old Haakon said, sitting on a wooden desk next to his father's portrait and two white candles. “As king, my father represented Norway and the Norwegian people with pride and joy, through visits around the country, at events here at the royal palace, and while working on Norway’s behalf around the world,” Haakon said. “I’m going to miss him. I’ll miss his laughter. His good-natured way of dealing with people and situations,” he added, trying to hold back his tears as he vowed to give everything for the country in the future as its new king. “And that means — in the ultimate sense — being willing to risk everything, even one’s life, for Norway’s freedom and independence.” Haakon adopted the motto “All for Norway,” which dates back to his great-grandfather. His wife became Queen Mette-Marit, while his oldest child, Ingrid Alexandra, became crown princess and heir to the throne. Earlier on Saturday, the new king and Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra welcomed Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and the presiding bishop of the Lutheran Church of Norway to the palace where King Harald's coffin was lying in state, the royal palace said in a statement. On Sunday morning, the Church of Norway is holding memorial services across the country, with the royal family expected to attend the service at Asker Church, southwest of Oslo, the palace said. Haakon is well acquainted with his royal obligations. As his father aged and his health declined in recent years, Haakon stepped in as regent on several occasions. His tasks in the near future will include shoring up support for the monarchy following controversies over his wife’s past contacts with deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his stepson’s rape conviction. A date for the funeral has not been set, but the country is officially in a state of mourning and some people decided to postpone celebrations such as weddings and baptisms until after the mourning period has passed, Norwegian public broadcaster NRK reported. Norway’s monarchy has old roots, tracing its origins to King Harald Fairhair in the ninth century. When Norway regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters in a national plebiscite approved restoring the monarchy. Today, the role is largely symbolic as power lies with an elected parliament, but the royal family retains celebrity and a role in promoting the wealthy nation around the world.

Takaichi faces rule-of-law scrutiny over US sanctions on ICC. TOKYO (Jiji Press) -- Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is under scrutiny regarding the country's commitment to the rule of law following U.S. sanctions against International Criminal Court President Tomoko Akane, the first Japanese to lead the organization. Initially, Takaichi merely said that the U.S. sanctions against Akane were "very regrettable." This led to criticism as the remark was perceived as a weak response. The focus is on whether Japan can dissuade the United States from seeking to "dismantle" the ICC. On Tuesday, Takaichi told reporters that the U.S. sanctions were "incompatible with the Japanese position and we take them seriously." "We must protect Ms. Akane and the precious organization of the ICC as the largest contributor to it," the prime minister also said. Japan values the rule of law and has consistently supported the ICC. The government is on high alert for further U.S. sanctions. If the ICC itself becomes a target, its operations could be severely affected. "The sanctions against the ICC are a crisis of the rule of law," Akane said at a press conference Wednesday. She urged the Japanese government to make "maximum efforts," including by engaging with the United States. The government plans to respond in close cooperation with Akane. On Friday, Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi held a telephone conversation with Akane to discuss the situation surrounding the ICC. However, it remains unclear how assertive Japan can be as the country has made its alliance with the United States the cornerstone of its diplomacy and security policy. The government has not protested or called for a withdrawal regarding the latest sanctions, which have drawn criticism even from the ruling Liberal Democratic Party. "We are engaging with the United States while saying what needs to be said," Motegi told a press conference Friday. However, a government official said, "We can't be too tough on the United States." Under the banner of the rule of law, the Takaichi administration has criticized China and Russia for attempting to change the status quo by force. If Japan turns a blind eye to threats to the rule of law out of consideration for the United States, its credibility could be significantly undermined. Public opinion is also scrutinizing the government's handling of the issue. "The prime minister's initial remarks drew various criticisms," a government official said, expressing concerns that any further impact on the Takaichi administration's approval ratings would be damaging.

Toddler stabbed to death by own father in Ilocos Sur. TAGUDIN, Ilocos Sur — A three-year-old child was allegedly stabbed to death by his own 29-year-old father in Barangay Lacong here on Friday, August 28, police said in a belated report. Police said the suspect, also a resident of this town, fled after the incident and is now the subject of a manhunt. Initial investigation disclosed that, before the incident, the victim’s grandmother and aunt reportedly heard the victim and the suspect talking to each other at around 1 a.m. on August 28. At around 11 a.m., the grandmother became suspicious after noticing that her grandchild had not come out of the room. She opened the door and found the child covered with a blanket. When she removed it, she saw blood on the victim’s chest. The child was immediately rushed to a hospital but was declared dead on arrival. The suspect had already fled the house when authorities arrived. Investigators said no bladed weapon believed to have been used in the killing was recovered from the crime scene. Police are conducting follow-up operations to locate and arrest the suspect.

Ontario premier answers Trump’s ‘Lake America’ with giant ‘Lake Ontario’ sign. TORONTO (AP) — Ontario Premier Doug Ford answered President Donald Trump’s “Lake America” decree Saturday with a billboard-sized message on the Canadian shoreline — “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” — as Canadian leaders met the move with ridicule rather than outrage. Wearing a Team Canada soccer jersey, Ford unveiled the sign near Grimsby, Ontario, and posed for photographs. The 24-by-12-foot (7.3-by-3.6 meter) sign stands on 6-foot (1.8-meter) legs, putting its top about 18 feet (5.5 meters) above the ground — roughly two stories high. The message is repeated in French, one The display followed Trump’s executive order directing U.S. federal agencies to call Lake Ontario “Lake America.” After months of tariffs, threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state and personal attacks on its leaders, the reaction in Canada has mixed defiance with mockery. Ford said Trump was trying to rename the lake because Ontario and Canada were “standing up for ourselves” and argued the name would outlast the president. “Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario,” Ford said in a video posted on social media. Canadians mock Trump Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew compared Trump to an aging rock band trying to revive an old hit “You know when a rock band is really over the hill and you see them like in a casino playing some song from like 50 years ago. I think that’s the part of Donald Trump’s presidency we’re at now, Like he thought they had a real hit, a real golden oldie, with the Gulf of Mexico,” Kinew said, referring to Trump's executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. “And he’s trying to bring back that, and he’s trying to play the hits for his base. But I think everybody here thinks it’s a little sad and it’s not his best work.” The mockery was not limited to politicians. Canadian historian Robert Bothwell was even more scathing. “The greatest country on earth takes this moron seriously?” Bothwell said. But Bothwell said the dispute was more serious than the jokes, arguing Trump’s broader aim was “to subordinate Canada and at best make it a colony, at worst absorb it into the United States.” Nelson Wiseman, professor emeritus at the University of Toronto, said Trump “would like Canada to act like a vassal state, but it refuses to do so. That irritates him.” Canada and the US trade barbs over collapsed talks The dispute comes as relations between the longtime allies worsen over trade. Negotiations collapsed last week, both governments accused the other of making late demands, and Canada announced retaliatory tariffs set to take effect next month. Trump’s order also came amid an escalating war of words with Ford. In an interview with The Associated Press earlier this week, Ford said Ronald Reagan would be “throwing up” over Trump’s tariff policies and “disgusted with President Trump.” Trump fired back by dismissing Ford’s comments as “bluster,” calling him Prime Minister Mark Carney’s “flunky” and mocking him as the “less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother” of the late Toronto Mayor Rob Ford. Trump continued promoting the new name Saturday, reposting a meme showing Canada geese with Trump-like blond hair firing rifles as they “protected” Lake America. Trump has repeatedly used maps to make political points. A “Gulf of America” map was displayed for a time beside the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office, and Trump has posted images depicting Canada as part of the United States or as the 51st state. Ontario name has Indigenous origins The name Lake Ontario comes from the Huron Indigenous people’s word “oniatarí:io,” which means “lake of shining waters.” The Canadian province of Ontario, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake. Wendat Nation Grand Chief Pierre Picard, whose people historically lived from the St. Lawrence Valley to the Great Lakes and whose language gave Lake Ontario its name, called Trump’s move an attempt to erase Indigenous history. “I want to tell him that it is unacceptable for us, as a nation, to have a president who can eradicate our history, our culture and our identity,” Picard said. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected the move, noting the lake’s Indigenous roots and that the name predates both Canadian Confederation and the U.S. Declaration of Independence. Trump cannot require Canada to adopt the new name.

Baguio City mayor warns residents against landslides caused by habagat. BAGUIO CITY – Baguio City Mayor Benjamin Magalong alerted residents to be prepared, be careful, and evacuate landslide-prone areas in connection with the ongoing rains caused by the Habagat. In PAGASA's August 30, 2026 Weather Advisory No.30, the province of Benguet, including Baguio City, will experience Orange Rainfall from 100-200 mm, while some parts of the Cordillera will experience 5-100 mm rainfall. Magalong also alerted responders of the City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (CDRRMC) to continue to attend incidents involving soil erosion, landslides, and fallen or leaning trees as persistent monsoon rains continue to affect the city. The prolonged rainfall has resulted in various incidents in different areas, prompting response teams to conduct assessments, clearing, mitigation, and other necessary interventions to ensure public safety. Among the recent incidents attended to by responders as of 12 noon Sunday, August 30, 2026, were: *Purok 3, Happy Hallow – A landslide and fallen boulder damaged a wall, window, and water line in the area. *Springhills, Loakan Apugan – Responders assisted in the installation of a tarpaulin over an area affected by soil erosion to help prevent further deterioration. *Purok Greenhills, Slaughter Compound – Soil erosion behind a single-storey house was first observed on August 9. No further movement was noted until the early morning of August 26, when rocks began falling and damaged the rear portion of the house. As of the latest assessment, the erosion continues to slowly encroach into the house. *Tiptop, Pacdal – A damaged drainage structure affecting nearby residences was attended to by responders for assessment and appropriate intervention. *Loakan Road, Loakan Proper – Responders addressed leaning trees along the road and undertook the cutting of an unstable eucalyptus tree to prevent possible hazards to motorists and pedestrians. The CDRRMC, led by Mayor Magalong, continues to closely monitor weather-related incidents and deploy response teams as needed. He reminded residents to remain vigilant as the rains continue, particularly those living near slopes, waterways, and other hazard-prone areas. Residents are urged to follow official advisories and immediately report dangerous conditions to the authorities by calling the emergency hotline 911 or the Baguio In My Pocket application.

Nepal warns of more possible floods as communities grapple with devastation. DHADING, Nepal (AP) — Authorities in Nepal are warning of possible fresh flooding on Sunday and urged residents in flood-affected districts to remain on high alert after water levels rose in the Bhotekoshi River. Flood warning notices were sent to people's phones throughout Sunday morning, as rescue crews worked to clear a major highway connecting Kathmandu to one of the areas worst-hit by Wednesday's catastrophic floods. In the town of Galchhi, a group of residents sought higher ground on a nearby bridge and watched as the river roared by. People pointed to enormous rocks that had been washed downriver during the earlier floods, as others standing on a suspension bridge over the water were warned off with whistles. Along the river entire homes, vehicles and farm tractors could be seen jutting from the thick grey-brown sediment that has enveloped entire villages in the worst-hit flood areas. Rice terraces along riverside had experienced landslides, dropping parts of their field into the river. The combined toll in Nepal and Tibet rose to 750 dead and over 3,000 people missing after the latest updates on Sunday. Nepal’s disaster agency said the death toll had climbed to 734 with 2,498 people missing, while Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, including over a hundred Nepalis and people from over a dozen countries. The latest warnings came after Chinese authorities informed their Nepalese counterparts of increased water flow upstream, Dharam Raj Uprety, chief executive of Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, told the Associated Press. But residents of the flood-hit villages said they were struggling to make sense of near-constant alarms they've received since the initial floods. “Sometimes they say a flood is coming, then we have to run again to higher ground, even at night. There is also rain,” said local resident Govind Shreshta. “It’s really difficult for me. I have a 72-year-old father and 70-year-old mom. I must carry them and I am exhausted. It’s going on like this for those who are still alive.” Large concrete and smaller suspension bridges were destroyed, leaving communities on the other side of the river less easy access. “Those that are there are now stuck there. Those who are here are stuck here. It’s going to be very difficult,” said Sattan Singh Tamang, 47, who was working near a bridge when Wednesday’s the floods came. Homes and businesses left intact after the flooding were still without electricity on Sunday, as twisted power line poles and wires lay tangled in the mud. Prithivi Highway is crucial supply route for food, fuel and other goods entering Kathmandu from other parts of the country. While most of the highway is operational, other parts still face repair challenges.

Japan to dispatch SDF helicopters to wildfire-hit Indonesia. TOKYO (Jiji Press) -- Japan will deploy three CH-47 transport helicopters of its Ground Self-Defense Force to Indonesia as part of an international emergency relief operation in response to the ongoing forest fires in the Southeast Asian country, Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi has said. The helicopters will be used for firefighting activities. This will be the first time for the SDF to conduct firefighting operations overseas. According to the Defense Ministry, around 600 personnel will participate in the relief mission. The Maritime SDF transport vessel Kunisaki, carrying the three helicopters, is expected to depart for Indonesia soon. Koizumi told reporters on Friday, "We will do everything possible to help prevent further expansion of the damage." Following a request for assistance from the Indonesian government, the Japanese government discussed possible support measures. On Friday, Koizumi ordered the commander of the SDF's Joint Operations Command to carry out the mission.

Student blinded in one eye after being bullied in Baguio. BAGUIO CITY – Parents are calling for justice for their 13-year-old son who went blind in one eye after he was punched by a 12-year-old student on August 20 in Barangay Quezon Hill Proper, Baguio City. The incident occurred at around 2:10 p.m. on August 20, according to an appeal sent by a family friend to Bombo Radyo Baguio and a police report sent to the office of City Director Ruel Tagel of the Baguio City Police Office. The incident was allegedly not given enough attention because it did not go viral, unlike the previous bullying incident in Pinsao Proper. The victim’s family is calling for justice, saying they were helpless because the response of the authorities was unacceptable to them. The family said it felt like authorities were paying more attention to the welfare of the boy who punched them than the victim, especially since he will have to live with the effects of losing his eyesight in one eye for the rest of his life. Medical records from the Baguio General Hospital and Medical Center showed that the victim was admitted on August 20 after being "suddenly punched in the face", with the impact focused on the left periorbital area. The hospital's clinical abstract stated that he complained of pain in his left eye and loss of vision. Doctors diagnosed him with a ruptured left globe and left periorbital contusion. He was discharged on August 23. According to Tagel, the reported incident is being thoroughly investigated, and authorities have begun handling the case under the juvenile justice system. He said the 12-year-old was immediately sent to the City Social Welfare and Development Office for assessment, intervention, and proper disposition under Republic Act 9344, or the Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act.

Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Fulbert Ngodji Analyst, Central Africa https://www.linkedin.com/in/fulbert-dg-ngodji-459054147/ Related Tags Chad Sudan On 22 August, the Chadian army accused its Sudanese counterpart of attacking a convoy in eastern Chad. In a televised statement , the army spokesman said Sudanese army aircraft and drones had pursued the trucks over 100km into Chad two days earlier before striking them in Mourdi department, Ennedi-Est province. Pro-Sudanese army online platforms circulated images purporting to show the army disabling several vehicles carrying supplies for the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the paramilitary group it has been fighting for control of Sudan since April 2023. The Sudanese army has not directly responded to the allegation, merely affirming its “respect for Chad’s sovereignty” in a 27 August statement . Open-source data and confidential sources have allowed Crisis Group to piece together a plausible account of what happened. A convoy of around 200 military pickup trucks reportedly left Libya and crossed Chad en route to Sudan. The Sudanese army or one of its allies then appears to have attacked the trucks near the Chadian border, as part of a months-long aerial campaign to disrupt RSF supply lines from Libya. About 70 vehicles tried to escape by crossing back into Chad, where they were destroyed. Satellite imagery showing smoke rising from the area seems to corroborate the Chadian army’s charge. It is unclear, however, who was driving the trucks and what they were carrying. The Chadian army did not address these questions. The conflict in Sudan has repeatedly spilled into Chad, primarily through an influx of refugees and, more recently, cross-border violence. Since December 2025, Chad’s eastern border has seen at least eleven incursions and drone strikes, which reportedly have killed about 30 civilians and soldiers. N’Djamena has typically sent military reinforcements or closed the border in response, but to this point it had refrained from blaming either of the main warring parties in Sudan. The 22 August statement is a departure from the previous caution, raising concerns that Chad will be drawn deeper into the civil war next door. Not only could Chad’s allegation sharpen tensions with the army-aligned authorities in Khartoum, but it could also reinforce perceptions that N’djamena has chosen sides in Sudan’s war, indirectly supporting the RSF. These perceptions are based on evidence that the United Arab Emirates has been using Chadian territory to provide the RSF with weapons and equipment. N’Djamena and Abu Dhabi have consistently denied these claims. Even so, escalation is unlikely: a confrontation would be costly for both N’Djamena and the Sudanese army. President Mahamat Déby is struggling to contain anger among his Zaghawa ethnic group, which has dominated Chad’s ruling elite since 1990. Many Zaghawa resent the government’s alleged backing of the RSF. The Sudanese army, meanwhile, controls Khartoum and much of central, northern and eastern Sudan, but remains locked in a war of attrition with no end in sight. Still, if the Sudanese army did in fact conduct the strike, its scale sets a dangerous precedent and could pave the way for more attacks by Sudanese belligerents, fuelling risks of a response by N’Djamena. Jailed Journalist in Azerbaijan Denied Medical Care. Click to expand Image Aytaj Ahmadova during a rally on International Women's Day, March 8, 2024 in Baku, Azerbaijan. © 2024 Aziz Karimov/Getty Images Azerbaijani authorities are refusing to allow a jailed journalist with a serious breathing disorder to see a specialist or to undergo diagnostic scans, her family and lawyer say, the latest sign of the deteriorating conditions for the country’s imprisoned journalists. Aytac Ahmadova, 32, who writes as Aytac Tapdig, is a reporter for the exiled outlet Meydan TV. She has been in pretrial detention at Kurdakhani Prison since December 6, 2024, when she was arrested with five Meydan TV colleagues in raids, days after Azerbaijan hosted the COP29 climate summit. She was initially charged with currency smuggling, and later other financial crimes. Her ongoing trial, alongside 11 other journalists and media workers, began in December 2025 and has no verdict date. Tapdig has a nasal condition and chronic breathing difficulties. A July 2026 letter from detention revealed that she had used 80 bottles of nasal spray and become dependent on them. The Penitentiary Service does not employ an ear, nose, and throat (ENT) specialist, she said. Her lawyer’s appeal to the Justice Ministry has gone unanswered, requests for relevant scans have been refused, and she has not received the results of earlier examinations. Under the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (the Nelson Mandela Rules), and consistently underscored by the European Committee on the Prevention of Torture by whom Azerbaijan is bound, prisoners are entitled to health care equivalent to that available to regular citizens. Withholding treatment can amount to ill-treatment. Following a February 18 hearing, Tapdig and two imprisoned colleagues were assaulted during a surprise cell raid. That month, open family visits at the facility were suspended. The Interior Ministry has imposed a travel ban on Tapdig's mother. In late June, Tapdig's telephone calls with friends were cut. Tapdig and her colleagues are facing disciplinary action after they shouted that journalism is not a crime during a May 1 court hearing. Tapdig is among 25 journalists Human Rights Watch has followed and documented since the current crackdown on media freedoms began in November 2023. Some have already been sentenced. Azerbaijani authorities should immediately provide Tapdig with appropriate medical care and disclose relevant information to her and her lawyer. They should investigate the February assault, drop all charges leveled against the journalists and release them. The European Union and the Council of Europe should publicly press Azerbaijani authorities on these cases.

Spain: Humanitarian and Rights Crisis in Ceuta. Click to expand Image Two of the migrants and asylum seekers who swam to Ceuta in July 2026, walk on Trampolín beach, August 2026. © 2026 José Antonio Sempere Gálvez for Human Rights Watch (Milan) – The Spanish government and local authorities in its North African enclave Ceuta should act urgently to provide adequate shelter to all migrants and asylum seekers living unsheltered since entering Ceuta from Morocco at the end of July, Human Rights Watch said today. The authorities should provide the opportunity to apply for asylum for those who want to. “Thousands of people have been in the streets in a legal vacuum, exposed to sexual violence and without adequate shelter, food, or sanitation for almost three weeks,” said Judith Sunderland, senior associate director for refugee and migrant rights at Human Rights Watch. “Despite the challenging situation, Spain should quickly mobilize sufficient resources to ensure humane and orderly management of the crisis for the good of migrants and Ceuta residents alike.” During a four-day research trip to Ceuta, from August 15 to 18, Human Rights Watch spoke with 76 migrants, including 42 individual interviews (37 adults and 5 unaccompanied children) and group or brief conversations with 34, including 4 unaccompanied children. Tens of thousands of migrants and asylum seekers swam from Morocco into Ceuta between July 30-31, and it is unclear how many remain in the city. Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska Gómez said on August 13 that 5,000 are still in Ceuta, while local organizations told Human Rights Watch there may be as many as 10,000. On August 17, Minister of Inclusion, Social Security and Migration Elma Saiz Delgado announced the installation of four tent camps in Ceuta with space for 1,500 adults, and authorities began transferring people to two sites on August 20. But they will not meet the need. Many people interviewed speculated that Spain’s government delayed assistance to convince people to return to Morocco. Humanitarian groups believe more than a thousand men and boys were living in makeshift huts on a city beach called Trampolín, with thousands more living on the streets, in a warehouse district near the Moroccan border, and the forested hills on the city’s edge. Roughly 700 to 750 women and girls are in two open-air sports facilities set up by neighborhood associations, while others are on the streets. The shortage of shower and toilet facilities means people are using parks, empty lots, and the sea. On August 3, the Spanish Red Cross started to distribute food at Trampolín beach; the government said on August 17 that it was handing out 4,000 food bags a day. Luna Blanca, a local charity, told Human Rights Watch they were distributing between 2,700 and 3,500 meals a day in five locations with government funding. Click to expand Image Men on the Trampolín beach, Ceuta, where more than a thousand migrants and asylum seekers camped in makeshift huts for almost three weeks after swimming to Spain’s enclave in North Africa from Morocco in July 2026. August 2026. © 2026 José Antonio Sempere Gálvez for Human Rights Watch Click to expand Image Migrants and asylum seekers gather for the once-daily food distribution at Trampolín beach, Ceuta, which means waiting hours in the sun for a bag of food. August 2026. © 2026 José Antonio Sempere Gálvez for Human Rights Watch “I went without food for the first two or three days; I only drank water,” said Mahmoud, a 36-year-old Palestinian from Gaza. “I stayed up in the mountains for 10 days before coming down to the beach with the others. It’s hardly a life, but I say alhamdulillah (praise be to God), it’s nothing compared to what my family is going through in Gaza.” As of August 20, Human Rights Watch saw no indication that Spanish authorities had begun any legal procedures or individual assessments of adults. While Moroccans appear to make up the majority of those who arrived in late July, Human Rights Watch also spoke with men and boys from Chad, Senegal, Somalia, Sudan, Tunisia, Yemen, Algeria, Syria, and Egypt. Many had spent years on arduous journeys and expressed their wish to apply for asylum in Spain. “I want to apply for asylum,” said Mohamed, a 20-year-old from Sudan. “But we don't have any information yet.” Click to expand Image Two of the migrants and asylum seekers who arrived in Ceuta in July 2026 wash their clothes in the sea at Trampolín beach, August 2026. © 2026 José Antonio Sempere Gálvez for Human Rights Watch Many Moroccan women spoke of escaping domestic abuse. Fatima, 47, from Tetouan, swam to Ceuta with her 11-year-old son to escape her abusive former husband. “I left my country not because I’m hungry, but because my husband is a drug addict; he beats me and my son,” she said. She showed a long scar on her arm where she said he cut her with a knife. Her attempts to report him to the Moroccan police, she said, were futile. Fatima went to the Ceuta police, but they told her to go to the warehouse district where hundreds are sleeping outdoors “until there is a solution.” Under European Union rules in place since mid-June, Spain should have already screened everyone, including security and health checks and a “preliminary vulnerability check” to identify stateless people, survivors of torture or other inhuman or degrading treatment, and people with “special needs,” under EU law. It is unclear whether Spain will resort to accelerated asylum border procedures, which could lead to swift rejections, including because asylum seekers were previously in Morocco, which the EU considers a “safe third country” where people should have applied for international protection. Moroccan nationals, including women alleging fear of domestic violence, risk return because of a “safe country of origin” readmission agreement with Spain. The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in Spain has urged authorities to provide information about the right to asylum and identify protection needs through proper screening. Migrants not needing international protection may be eligible for Spain’s Humanitarian Assistance Program. At Trampolín beach, most men and boys were living in huts they built from sticks, cardboard, and trash bags. A few groups had tents. In a warehouse district near the border with Morocco, hundreds of people—including families with young children, single mothers with children, and unaccompanied children—were sleeping on cardboard. Click to expand Image A woman tidies around her makeshift shelter in the warehouse district on Ceuta where hundreds have been sleeping rough since swimming from Morocco into Spain’s enclave, August 2026. © 2026 José Antonio Sempere Gálvez for Human Rights Watch Residents’ associations in El Principe and Sidi Embarek neighborhoods set up improvised shelters in two open-air sports venues to provide safety for women and girls amid reports of sexual violence. Authorities set up one canopy tent in each location, but most are living under strung-up tarps. Volunteers in both locations said that authorities had transferred as many as 200 girls from the El Principe site to government-run facilities in Ceuta. Four emergency-room doctors said they had treated a total of two women and six girls, including one 14-year-old Moroccan and one 11-year-old from an unidentified African country, for sexual assault and rape. A 25-year-old Moroccan woman said a Spanish-speaking man raped her the night she arrived; she has not reported the rape to the police. The Ceuta public prosecutor’s office said it had received 13 cases of sexual assault between July 30 and August 17, with the majority of victims not city residents. The situation for unaccompanied children is particularly concerning, Human Rights Watch said. There are no reliable statistics on how many may be in the city. A source in the Ceuta government, which under Spanish law is responsible for unaccompanied children, said they had taken charge of 1,385 as of August 18. The same day, the Interior Ministry said the police had registered 2,168 unaccompanied children. Click to expand Image Food distribution by Luna Blanca, a Ceuta nongovernmental organization, at the warehouse district in Ceuta where hundreds of migrants and asylum seekers are sleeping rough, August 2026. © 2026 José Antonio Sempere Gálvez for Human Rights Watch Click to expand Image A migrant collects a container of lentil soup at a food distribution by Luna Blanca, a Ceuta nongovernmental organization, in a warehouse district in Ceuta where hundreds have been sleeping rough for weeks, August 2026. © 2026 José Antonio Sempere Gálvez for Human Rights Watch Two schools converted into temporary shelters for children need to be vacated before the school year starts in early September; authorities are trying to identify alternative sites despite objections from residents. Spanish media reported on August 19 that the youth ministry was working to transfer of 500 unaccompanied girls from Ceuta to other parts of Spain. At the end of day on July 31, the Spanish government said the majority of those who swam to Ceuta in the previous 48 hours had returned to Morocco voluntarily, amid reports that Spanish security forces rounded people up in trucks to take them to the border. Spanish authorities officially recorded 82 deaths, while there may have been at least 67 on the Moroccan side according to the Spanish group Caminando Fronteras. While many local associations and individual residents have aided migrants, tensions in the city of 85,000 people have sparked concerns over possible violence. Halima Ahmed of Luna Blanca called it a “catastrophic situation without precedents…There is so much uncertainty and that generates fear among residents, and the problem is when fear turns to hatred.” Mohamed El Harrak of the nonprofit group EXMENAS expressed concern about a climate of hate, saying the city “needs action before this explodes. The priority is humanitarian aid. Ceuta can’t do it alone.” Spanish authorities should urgently mobilize sufficient resources to ensure adequate reception, whether in Ceuta or elsewhere in Spain, and individual assessments with access to legal advice in language people can understand, Human Rights Watch said. The European Convention on Human Rights, to which Spain is a party and which applies in Ceuta, prohibits collective expulsions. Spain should ensure full examination of asylum claims and refrain from deporting third-country nationals, such as Sudanese or Somalis, to Morocco. Authorities should use multi-disciplinary age assessments to identify unaccompanied children. EU and Spanish law require that unaccompanied children may only be deported to their home country following an individualized assessment taking into account their best interest and the conditions upon return. “Spanish authorities should not let populist calls for mass summary deportations prevent them from acting in accordance with their obligations under international law,” Sunderland said. “Nor should Spanish authorities be deterred from conducting fair, individual assessments of protection claims and treating all migrants with dignity.”

Chad: Political Opponents Freed. Click to expand Image Demonstrators in Paris, France wave Chadian flags during a rally calling for the release of Succès Masra, May 31, 2025. © 2025 Umit Donmez / Anadolu via AFP (New York) – The Chadian authorities should vacate or set aside the conviction of Succès Masra, the former Chadian prime minister and main opposition leader, Human Rights Watch said today. Masra was released from prison on August 15, 2026, after receiving a presidential pardon. His pardon and those of eight other political opponents led to their release from prison. However, their convictions for conduct that was legitimate political expression still stand and need to be set aside so they can continue to participate in politics. “The release of Masra and other political opponents is good news,” said Lewis Mudge, Central Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “But to be clear, Masra was arrested on trumped-up charges in an attempt to silence him. The Chadian authorities should go beyond the presidential pardon and ensure that his conviction is set aside.” Masra, who served as Chad’s prime minister from January to May 2024, was arrested on May 16, 2025, after running against then-transitional President Mahamat Idriss Déby in the 2024 presidential election. Prosecutors accused him of inciting hatred and violence following the deaths of 42 people in intercommunal clashes on May 14 in Mandakao, Logone Occidental province, in the country’s southwest. While clashes between herders and farmers are common in southern Chad, intercommunal violence has become more acute over the past several years, resulting in scores of deaths. Masra was charged with inciting hatred and violence through social media posts. Following the Logone Occidental violence, Masra had expressed condolences to the victims, stating that “no Chadian’s life should be taken for granted.” Masra, who pleaded not guilty, was tried alongside 74 co-defendants, all accused of collaboration in the deaths at Mandakao. While at least 9 of the defendants were released at trial, the remainder received 20-year prison sentences. The 65 co-defendants convicted alongside Masra are still in prison and should also be released, and their convictions should be set aside, Human Rights Watch said. Human Rights Watch was told that some of the co-defendants may have died in detention but was unable to confirm this information. Eight leaders from Chad’s main opposition coalition, the Political Actors’ Consultation Group, known by its French acronym GCAP, were pardoned at the same time as Masra. The GCAP leaders were serving eight-year prison sentences following their convictions on charges of rebellion for planning a protest march. Two of the eight GCAP leaders had earlier been released on health grounds. The Supreme Court dissolved the GCAP in April 2026, alleging that it was involved in illegal activity. Masra had appealed his conviction to the Supreme Court, but the court upheld his conviction and 20-year sentence in May. While the presidential pardons granted to Masra and the GCAP leaders led to their release, their convictions and financial penalties remain intact. Masra and his co-defendants still have an outstanding fine to the total of 1 billion Central African francs (approximately US$1.8 million), imposed at the same time as their prison sentences. The standing conviction also means he retains his criminal record and leaves him ineligible to run for office. The convictions should therefore be set aside or revised in accordance with Chadian law, Human Rights Watch said. Masra’s case was significant. He and his supporters from the opposition party Les Transformateurs (The Transformers) faced threats prior to the May 2024 elections, in which Masra ran against then-transitional President Gen. Mahamat Idriss Déby. After Déby was declared the winner, his presidency ended a transitional period that started in 2021, following the death of his father, then-President Idriss Déby Itno, who was killed while fighting an armed group a day after being re-elected to his sixth term. A government crackdown on freedom of expression and association has at times been very violent. After Idriss Déby Itno’s death, security forces used excessive force, including live ammunition fired indiscriminately, to disperse opposition-led demonstrations across the country. Several protesters were killed. Authorities detained activists and opposition party members, and security forces beat journalists covering the protests. On October 20, 2022, security forces fired live ammunition at protesters—killing and injuring scores of demonstrators—and beat and chased people into their homes. Hundreds of men and boys were arrested, and many were taken to Koro Toro, a high security prison 600 kilometers away from N’Djamena. Several detainees died en route, some due to lack of water. At Koro Toro, protesters suffered further abuse, including severe ill-treatment by other detainees. In October 2023, dozens of members of Les Transformateurs were arrested in the lead up to a constitutional referendum to allow Mahamat Déby to run as a candidate after the transition. While the presidential pardon decree presented the releases of Masra and the eight GCAP leaders as a gesture toward national unity and reconciliation, the authorities have shown intolerance of debate or dissent, including open discussions about Chad’s past. While the leaders have been pardoned, their arrests formed part of a broader government crackdown against perceived critics and opponents, Human Rights Watch said. “The charges against Masra lacked credibility and any evidential basis, and he should never have been arrested and detained in the first place,” Mudge said. “The Chadian authorities should bring this matter to a close, vacate his conviction, and let him exercise his rights and re-engage in politics.”

Governments Should Protect Environmental Defenders from Violence and Repression. Click to expand Image Supporters of imprisoned environmental activists stage a protest during their appeal hearing outside of the Royal Courts of Justice, London, January 29, 2025. © 2025 Sipa via AP Images As space for environmental advocacy rapidly shrinks, Indigenous peoples, climate activists, and land defenders increasingly face harassment, criminalization, and repression for protecting lands, ecosystems, and communities from environmental harm. The use of violence, intimidation, and threats to silence environmental defenders is an urgent challenge. Human Rights Watch Submission on Environmental Defenders for Sixth Report of the Special Rapporteur on the Human Right to a Healthy Environment Against this backdrop, the UN Special Rapporteur on the right to a healthy environment is compiling a report on environmental defenders worldwide, to which Human Rights Watch submitted input on August 19. In Brazil, HRW has extensively documented how criminal networks engaged in illegal deforestation, mining, and land-grabbing threaten and sometimes kill Indigenous people, small farmers, and environmental agents who stand in their way. HRW also documented police beating defenders peacefully protesting mining in Indonesia. Environmental defenders face governments’ mounting efforts to criminalize peaceful protest. While the United Kingdom and Australia have in recent years passed draconian laws criminalizing peaceful protests, countries such as Vietnam and Turkey have used broad legislation to harshly punish climate activists. In Indonesia, authorities prosecuted and wrongly punished hundreds of Indigenous activists and those protesting deforestation and environmental damages, including prosecutions for “spreading communism.” Labeling environmental defenders as terrorists or criminals, governments have also restricted advocacy by attacking civil society.
